There are many wonderful people in this organisation, and many of them are doing everything they can to reinvent and reboot banking from the inside. If you’re looking for a first job or place to build on your basic banking knowledge, then this is the opportunity you’ve been waiting for! 
Would recommend for grads and someone new to the industry. Also, if you’re terrible at your job, you should be able to find somewhere to hide in this organisation.
cons:
An incredibly top heavy organisation with plans to offshore everything but the vending machines. 
The long queue for the top, feels more like a slowly grinding treadmill, which only rewards a certain ethnic, gender mix. If you’re male and experienced, you’re likely to die before you’re promoted. Beyond that, you’re likely to be promoted before you receive a pay rise. Sadly, if you stay more than a year, you’ll be forced to watch many great people coming and leaving. This is a hard pill to swallow, whilst some of the longer standing untouchable staff languish in long periods of absenteeism and regularly miss “team” deadlines.

advice: It needs to be clearer as to who is pulling their weight and who isn't. Some talented juniors have left because there was more opportunity elsewhere. If the company is to be dynamic, then an meritocratic environment needs to be fostered.
pros:
1) The base pay is OK-good and the health benefits and pension contributions are good-excellent. BUPA is the health provider and they were excellent. 

2) There are some fantastic colleagues who are really talented engineers. 

3) The offices are generally very pleasant. 

4) Some of the engineering work is really interesting and can be exciting.

5) If you get a good/supportive manager, you can boost your career growth in a shorter time span.
cons:
1) Is there ever a month that goes by in which Deutsche Bank isn't in the news for money laundering? It's demoralising working for an organisation that has a nefarious history and continues to be involved in dodgy activities. With the hundreds of millions spent on KYC processes at DB, it's incredible that such crimes continued to still occur very frequently. 

2) The resource planning that I witnessed was at times absolutely absurd. It got to the point where some teams were incredibly stretched working on key deliverables with tight deadlines and with a small team. And yet, DB hired external consultants on several ocassions who would be paid extortinate sums of money to come up with 'digital transformation' ideas that would be executed by DB engineers. So, the company is paying at least twice. That inconsistent approach to resourcing seemed to happen frequently. 

3) Some colleagues, especially around the VP level, are medicore and there's a layer of fat who enjoy good benefits which they realistically wouldn't get elsewhere who just stay and do just above the minimum while some really talented juniors get less benefits and tougher objectives. So, it's not really ultra meritocratic although if you really, really want it, you'll tend to get it. Also, at below VP level, no bonuses are paid. 

4) Also, the obsession from the senior management and board to get all employees, at least in Germany, COVID vaccinated and describing it as a 'moral obligation' in internal memos was creepy and a gross overreach. How about let employees decide for themselves what is best for their bodies or is that concept too hard for a German company to understand?

5) I experienced some super crazy politics that meant that collective objectives weren't met. At a VP+ level, things can become a bit machiavellian in that what's in the interests for the company aren't necessarily in the interests for your own personal career growth but that's an elephant in the room that everyone ignores. 

An example may be that a certain legacy system wasn't migrated to a new system because it has some critical functionality and the team supporting the application were fired very quickly in the past for some unknown reasons. By migrating the system and saving the company money, you wouldn't be able to have X budget to keep maintaining that sytem and having a bigger team. So, you would lose headcount and budget by doing what's a positive thing for the company. So objectives need to be better aligned. Also, teams would compete with each other for 'territory' as that would bring in more budget so things get quite odd when officially, you're in the same boat but unofficially, you're conspiring how to 'one up' them all the time. 

6) DB engineering tends to build things with the best of intentions and then some new top dog will come in and make wholesale changes, like firing an entire team that supports/maintains some applications, that make the past 2 years of hard work totally pointless and redundant. Technology and ways of doing things do indeed change but the lack of a consistent approach / consistent goal over different eras of Managing Directors results in a bit of a headless chicken effect.

7) It is getting much better but diversity at the top level is still lop-sided. There are measures being taken to address this but there's a long way to go.

summary: Career development paralysed for the foreseeable future
advice:
Hire capable COOs, hold them to account and actively manage them if they don’t introduce robust & reasonable governance.
Shake up the HR department, bring in new blood who are interested in challenging management & developing people so that the bank has the capability it needs to rebuild.
pros: International exposure & in the past a great many collegiate & talented colleagues all pulling in the same direction.
cons:
Senior management have buried their heads in the sand for too many years regarding the cost challenge that the business continues to face. Forced in the last couple of years (quite rightly) by John Cryan & shareholders to finally tackle this issue the (unfortunately) necessary restructures have been managed very badly. Senior management in some divisions have made short term panicked decisions ultimately prioritising saving themselves & favourite senior long servers (high cost employees in high cost locations). They have made lower cost mid to junior level employees redundant or just moved “deckchairs around on the deck of the Titanic”. Many have not made decisions based on robust business reasons. In some isolated examples it has been worse still. I have seen examples of  totally unethically miss managing people & making the environment so toxic that people have left of their own accord nearly broken.
This of course has failed to tackle the cost challenge and has resulted in multiple badly managed rounds of redundancies within months in the same areas. This has left moral very low for those left and has blocked career paths for years to come. This does not set the bank up for success and will drive down moral further over the medium to long term. 
COOs are in the main unskilled in their field and have little understanding, control or governance in their areas. There is no sign of this improving, only more responsibility being delegated to already failing individuals.
HR are being “dumbed down” to administrators & processors with strong capable people leaving this department in large numbers in the last 18 months.
These two issues (COO & HR combined) mean that management do not have capable or trusted advisors & are also not challenged to make short, medium AND long term cost decisions whilst restructuring by humanely exiting the right mix of people to allow the business to rebuild sustainably.

VP/AVP could even be very inexperienced, having come from the local market with a non-investment banking background. 
Good regional employer, but not what you'd expect for an IB, if moving with experience from Ldn etc, you might not enjoy it much. 
If you join DB Birmingham, and try to move to London - they'll keep you on your Birmingham salary, very hard to get that changed once in there.

summary: Potential to be a good place to work
advice:
Listen to your employess. 
Look after your talent before they leave. 
Stop protecting senior\middle management that are obviously not fit for the roles they do
pros:
Benefits package
CSR
Name
Internal job mobility is promoted
Global presence, opportunities available to work in most key deutsche bank hubs
cons:
Poor senior management - Severe lack of direction, some are promoted not on merit but on who they know.

Worryingly, there are some senior managers, especially in technology who are protected by senior MD's. This "allows" them to behave in any manner they wish, resulting in a bullying culture and some very talented people leaving the bank.

Difficult Promotion process - Although in technology there is a more structured promotion process, the management in charge are not always the right people to make the right decisions. Promotions should be based on meritocracy and the persons ability to work at that level. I agree that a SME that struggles to work with others is a difficult candidate to promote and justifiaby needs to improve this aspect if they are to be promoted. 
There are many examples of employees who get promoted based on length of service, surely something any tier 1 investment bank should not do if they are to remain competitive.

summary: Great Company, Lots of Opportunities and Great Team Ethos
advice:
- Annual survey is helpful - Take notice and act on more of the feedback 
- Keep the projects well structured/defined and logical 
- Incentivise international collaboration more
- Hire more engineers 
- Keep up with the environmentally friendly investments
pros:
- Training available for anything you can think of
- Flexible working
- Salary 
- Dental and Health insurance 
- Partnership with google (year 2020) means all IT systems have updated and they are awesome 
- Opportunity to travel abroad for assignments depending on your division 
- Lots of smart people willing to help you go further in your professional career
- Many mechanical/electrical/software engineers in one place which means the projects are always logical and well structured 
- Opportunities to volunteer in different countries and/or charities of your choice
- Costbase has reduced meaning the bank is lean and on a upward trajectory
cons:
- The work can sometimes be too much European/American focused 
- The hours can be long if you are not careful and get into the habit
- Nature of the work means it's located in expensive cities - so rent is a fortune 
- You get used to working in finance and may never return to your field

advice: Cost cutting and moving jobs out to lower cost locations such as Birmingham, Jacksonville and Manila should not be key focus of management. There are factors such as lost of knowledge and expertise to consider too. Adding in additional layers within a work flow is just causing more work for ourselves.
pros:
- Work life balance
- Good benefits (not salary or bonus though)
- The nicest colleagues you can think of who are genuinely nice, helpful sincere people.
cons:
- Politics: people who are favoured by management are "safe" from jobs cut and new roles will be created for them to keep them onshore ie NY, London and Singapore
- Too focused on cost cutting, only aim of management
- Internal mobility is very very rare
- Very bad bonus in operations
- A million applications / systems which are either not functioning as they ought to be after all the massive investment pouring into it. 
- Some of the senior management (MD level) has no clue to what the department they are overseeing is about, thus really easy for them to say move jobs to lower cost locations without thinking of the implications

summary: There are better places to work
advice:
You need to work hard at making this bank an employer of choice, try competing in best place to work at - may encourage culture change and developing some empathy for your staff that spend more hours at your institution than with their loved ones.
Cut the bureaucracy
Cut the politics - the investment bankers have taken over the ship , now give it some strong leadership in the ranks and set a course that has all stakeholders' buy-in
Get rid of the 5s and 6s and start promoting 9s and 10s
If you want good people, and you want to keep them, you have to pay them
pros:
Global brand recognised by clients and investors facilitating winning mandates over competitors
Safe pair of hands in turbulent markets especially Europe
Prestige
Good learning ground for new starters
cons:
Not a great corporate culture. Way too much bureaucracy. 
Too many weak managers and mediocre senior people
This bank is NOT a meritocracy so if you are mid level and bright it will be years before you are either promoted or properly remunerated. T/O of star staff quite high at present.
Compensation and bonus pretty poor by market standards

summary: Great people but has the issues of a badly managed large corporation
advice:
Start rewarding loyalty.

This is a large organisation with a top down approach to HR and communication. Give more power to managers regarding staff, decisions can't be made by people who do not know you.

Reduce the silo nature within divisions and promote better relationships.
pros:
Purely depends on your team, your manager sets the tone and can either make your experience great or not want to come in.

Easy to build a network across countries and divisions.

Front office are very friendly but this varies by desk.
cons:
If you're a new hire you're fine, Deutsche does not keep salary at market rate so does not rewards loyalty.

There is high turnover in finance and don't be surprised if your team is 90% contractors.

People are hired without the right skill set on much higher than they should be.

Dependent on division some senior management see you purely as an asset and not a person.

The systems are horrendous as highlighted in the press.

There are not enough junior staff coming through the ranks which means you may spend more time doing menial tasks.

summary: Exciting and Challenging Work Place With Some Downsides
advice: Ensure that the values and beliefs of the Bank are actually imprinted into the culture, everyone can recite them but they not always put into practice.
pros:
Exciting and challenging environment with a lot of opportunities to be involved in additional projects or work streams.
There is a strong culture of encouraging people to be innovative and to take ownership for those innovations.
There are a large number of inspiring, smart and hardworking people who are a pleasure to work with.
Very good opportunities for training, self development, coaching and mentoring.
cons:
Constant reorganisation within the company which rarely bring any actual improvements.
Very hub centric (London, New York etc) with opportunities and benefits much reduced in other locations of the same country.
Archaic and complicated processes exist across the board.
The promotion process happens once a year and it can be very difficult to get promoted regardless of how well a person has performed. People can be pigeon holed into a role where visibility and opportunity are not available and they are then overlooked
There is an expectation of long and unsocial hours with little acknowledgement or reward.

summary: Chaotic culture, great people, poor leadership from senior management but improving
advice: Stay the course of the recent reorganisation initiative but minimise further churn until it beds down properly.  Seek to retain your better people who are feeling extremely undervalued at the moment.
pros:
Teamwork and within and accross teams is effective and productive with little no politics getting in the way, very much a one bank, one team attitude.

Senior management appear to have recognised how under invested IT has been for some time and are making many of the right sort of changes to process and people management.  There are lots of signs of improvement but it's slow and painful.
cons:
Lots of carryover from the silos of old where IT would be highly aligned with the business group they cover and not at all with the wider IT direction if one could be said to exist.  Though this is changing it's a big culture shift.

Base salaries tend to be lower than competing banks.  Very difficult to be promoted internally - many people appear to leave to take more senior positions outside of the firm.

summary: Deutsche Bank is made up of many seperate businesses. In the GBS/GTO morale in 2011 is diminishing
advice:
Consider your workforce and their potential rather than how they appear on a P&L
Make joined up decisions - the franchise could be a far stronger internal partnership than it is today
pros:
Diversity of workforce
Compensation
Global mandate, breadth of coverage
Depth of responsibility
cons:
The GBS/GTO Division Operating Model vision is focussed firmly on cost reduction - it's execution of this strategy is aggressive
Multiple / frequent management changes create lack of continuity
Mentality of some key players can be political versus practical - seemingly this is rewarded
Having been at the firm for 10+ years I am delighted with the career development DB has provided me with - I would not however recommend DB as an employer of choice now, in 2011

summary: Large organisation with some excellent but also at times average employees
pros:
Global powerhouse that has some truly exceptional talent. 
Work-life balance will vary depending on your division/team. For front office function expect 12 hour average working days. 
Top level leadership on the whole appears to have the right intentions but success of implementation remains uncertain. 
From experience DB typically will give young talent the chance to shine.
cons:
Despite many of years of integration efforts, teams remain siloed in comparison to other banks. 
- Inter team moves can be extremely challenging (e.g. FX sales to rates trading) 
- Politics can get intense at more senior levels with disproportionate amount of time spent on internal negotiations.
- Some very aggressive individuals on the trading floor

Away from the siloes, rest of the "cons" are unlikely different to investment banks.

summary: Steep learning curve, changing and dynamic environment, on the forefront of change and evolution
advice: Invest and seek out more younger candidates who have potential and hinger to grow, nurture and support the development and they will soon blossom into strong minded, smart young professionals with the right guidance and support
pros: Very professional, inspires growth and development, motivates personal growth, inspirational leaders, tools to excel are easily located. Self starter culture no hand holding which is good as it pushes you to drive yourself further. Amazing experience would love to return one day.
cons: If you are a temp you can only stay for maximum of 45 weeks until you have to be made perm or leave. Extensive screening - dig very deep and fill every single week gap you may have (took about 2weeks)

summary: DB is a wonderful place to work
advice: Keep on track and remove some of the dead wood. I would also initiate a 360 PMO service
pros: Progression is on merit which is wonderful if you're good at what you do, also being able to move between divisions / offices is great. Personnally I have loved every minute of being at DB (currently for 5 years) and would recommend the bank to others. Hard work is required but hours are not as insane as other banks I have worked for (namely a large american one!)
cons: Political environment and slow to get action quickly. PMO activity is limited to manager feedback only where I feel a full 360 review is a lot more beneficial to the overall picture.

summary: Depending on the division, can be exciting but lack of stability makes it hard to establish yourself (mid-senior level)
advice: Please create a leaner, more efficient universal bank that focuses on its true strengths. Make the staff feel more empowered by rewarding those with exemplary behaviour and punishing bad ones.
pros:
- A truly diverse workplace
- Reasonably meritocratic: base salary roughly in line with industry average, but salary can bump up your total comp if you do a good job
- Better work-life balance compared to other banks
cons:
- Intransparent promotion process
- A lot of politics at D and MD level
- Serious lack of organisational stability, which makes staff feel very insecure and unsettled
- Very few female senior managers
- Town halls are very generic and not very meaningful
- Internal career mobility can be encouraged more

advice: Concentrate on making sure that all the IT systems are brought up to par with those of DB's peers. Make sure the 2020 strategy is actually executed well!
pros: The bank is generally involved in all the good deals/underwritings and seems to have the resources to be one of the best banks in Europe. I am optimistic about the new CEO and strategy, and see an effort on senior management's part to create a cultural change. Decent salaries. The potential sale of Postbank could make things a lot better.
cons: The IT systems are not good and result in some time wasting. The bank has in the past been good at creating strategies for short and mid terms horizons, but not so good at executing them.

summary: Once great, struggling to resolve mass fragmentation caused by previous short-term strategies
advice: Remove unnecessary middle management, pay more attention to the people who do the hard work and are looking to consolidate and provide the efficiencies that are desperately needed to comply with the regulators and to reduce the cost-base.
pros: One of the most forward thinking and technically innovative banks of the early to mid 2000's with many hard working, intelligent and well meaning people.
cons: Corporate mentality of divide and conquer and to compete against and out-perform peers, as well as questionable re-organisation attempts has left the bank incredibly fragmented and unstable, from front to back office, technology and operations - particularly technology. The lack of governance will cost Deutsche Banks position as a tier 1 global contender.

summary: Solid company with solid values and looks likely to ride out the storm!
pros:
Enjoyable work with a very good work-life balance. There are appreciative managers who understand how to get the best from their directs.
The bank looks to be progressively engaging in new technologies and pushing hard to maintain a lead with its banking platform.
There appears to be global opportunities and good career development for those who seek it.
cons:
Slow to move in new directions. Focus towards reducing risk going forwards is often seen to be paralysing and (in some cases) appears to be reducing the motivation of (some) staff.
A few too many clock-watchers and a few pieces of dead wood lying around the place, but generally these people don't seem to get in the way too often.

advice: They have a difficult job, but treat their employees as adults. Don't censor difficult news, and don't try and spin the delivery. Be honest.
pros:
Reasonable amount of autonomy. Some very good people. Some interesting projects and technology initiatives, although their scope is not always as widespread as you hope. 
Some confidence that John Cryan is the right person for a very difficult job. He seems honest and upfront.
cons:
Feels like everything is being cut back. Once had aspirations to be a top tier institution, now feels 2nd or 3rd rate. 
Senior management have changed so much in a short space of time which means there is a lot of review and validation of existing work. When will we get around to execution?

summary: Great people, but plenty of bureaucracy
advice: * Stop using "regulations are complex in this area" as an excuse to not get anything done. Other similar organisations have already done it.
pros:
* People that make up the immediate software development teams are really great and friendly
* People are more than willing to share and teach skills
cons:

* Interactions between different departments can be challenging, and you have to navigate yourself through the different fiefdoms
* Plenty of paperwork and archaic processes to get many things done. 
* As the workforce gets smaller, there are more overworked people that you need to deal with when going through said paperwork and processes.

summary: Mixed bag, great place to join to learn stuff, but not a very good place to grow
advice: I think the management knows this already but they are doing this as a strategy so let me repeat what they already know. DB Management our biggest strength is our people, please please for haven's sake pay them properly. Pay i dont believe can be based on titles, PMO grades or some stupid measure that you feel fits all sizes. We work really hard and sorry to say work and comp don't seem to in sync at DB. I believe we are at  the right place to launch DB to a completely different level and please don't mess this up, believe me if pay goes up 5% i am sure our stock holders (mostly actively traded index funds and institutional holders) will barely notice, you know what's the right thing to do, don't let other firms (or govt's) perception dictate our policy.
pros:
Deutsche Bank's biggest asset is its people, the place is highly technical, knowledgeable, friendly.
Managers are open, honest. They also strive to maintain good work life balance.
cons: As mentioned above in Pros Deutsche Bank's biggest asset is its people, they are nice and technical. One problem with that is that its very difficult for management to understand that they have a really nice team and at times take that for granted (esp around comp time). This strategy is bound to back fire and once they lose good people it will become obvious to the management what's wrong with the strategy. More important is the fact that these good people would join competitors and hence DB will lose a lot in the long term.

cons: Not much as management is proactively tackling weaknesses

summary: Great Organisation with less red tape than most banks
pros:
Great team members and support 
pay is relatively good
cons: I didn't really notice much cons during my time there

summary: A company which is too large to be effectively managed but has a great brand
advice: As mentioned above, Senior management need to get the resourcing balance right - they spend too much money covering their backs by spending money on audit whilst they need to spend money on core functions such as technology.  Secondly attrition is a major concern - even in the current market environment (August 2008), collegues are leaving voluntarily.  Thirdly, there are far too many contractors and consultants employed at the bank.  These should be reduced as it is often the case that key contractors are kept as they "know too much" about critical systems.  Finally, Senior Management should seek to "westernise" the company.  The bank is still too bureaucratic and Germanic for the 21st century.
pros: The Deutsche Bank brand is brilliant - it is widely respected to DB's clients and because of this, it is also highly respected in the job markets.  The name on your CV, particularly if you can mention investment banking related experience, is worth a great deal.  In my opinion, the best reason to work for DB is it's global brand name.  Compared to other investment banks, its salary is competitive.  Another great reason to work for Deutsche Bank in the London office is the work life balance.  Unlike other investment banks, it understands that you have a life outside work!  For example, the social networks such as the family network are very active.
cons: Although Deutsche Bank boasts of a "one bank" culture, this is far from the truth.  The 1 bank brand is strong and it is worth recognising that there are roughly 80,000 employees at the firm; many of those work in the retail arm.  Although the retail business keeps things going in a downturn, it makes the firm far too large to manage.  Senior management is far too Germanic in their approach and fill your day with unproductive administration.  For example, technology and business audits are continually carried out but due to cost constraints, resourcing is so tight that there is no time to address these.  Some areas of the bank thrive but others consistently fail.

summary: Don't expect to be rewarded if you work in Technology.
advice: Pay people who work in Technology at least the market rate and provide them with performance related bonuses. If you pay peanuts, you get monkeys.
pros:
Technology in Deutsche Bank is way behind pretty much every one of its competitors. Thus, if you join technology you can be a part bringing it up to speed with the competition, and gain lots of responsibility in the process.

Hours are 9-5.
cons:
Compensation is exceptionally poor for people who work in technology. Bonuses are entirely politics based. It doesn't matter how hard you work. You might come up with a trading algorithm or technology enhancement that enables the trading desk to increase PnL by 50% to £1m, but don't expect that to be reflected in your bonus. You're still getting a fixed 20% so my best advice is to go home at 5 and not make the extra effort.

The business side still has absolute control over the budget, changing it widely from +/- 10% EACH quarter. It's impossible to plan any kind of stable headcount.

Management is poor. If you come up with a great idea in DB make sure you keep it to yourself, because EVERYONE will steal it and give you no credit whatsoever.

There are lots of opportunities in DB, but no one is going to help you take them. You've got to play political games all the time.

The graduate scheme is pretty awful. HR have made the assumption that if you're a graduate you know nothing about either banking or technology. I learnt nothing in the time I had training. You also get lumbered with two "Change Management" projects, which are essentially a load busy work and a waste of time. You teams management won't give you support in doing this so you're going to end up working weekends on it.

advice: Fairer promotion and rewards to internal employees with greater ability for employees to voice their desire to move without fear of being punished.
pros: Wide range of responsibilities and roles with plenty of face time with front office. This has brought about opportunities of moves into Front Office
cons: Lots of politics within the bank and a culture of paying a lot more external recruits and contractors whilst under paying the internal employees

summary: Good springboard into a financial career - but be prepared to be flexible and aware of setbacks.
advice: Take a serious review against your competitors and other organisations within the industry and the environments their employees work in and apply these to DB. Move away from the hierarchy as it is making DB incredibly toxic.
pros:
1. Some teams have a good ‘family feel’ work ethic and there are some genuinely good people.
2. Good internship opportunities with internal mobility widely championed.
3. Good external speaker events and lots of opportunities for self-directed development/networking.
4. Opportunities to learn new parts of the bank outside of day job.
5. Volunteering and charity events widely encouraged. Some good internal campaigns to increase moral during challenging times the bank is under.
6. Defined quarterly performance process although this is relatively standard.
7. Good 30-day holiday allowance with the opportunity to buy 5 more days. Some teams have dress down Friday, giving a sense of work-life balance.
8. Some very proactive initiatives and senior managers widely championing such programmes.
cons:
1. DBOI contracts not as good as AG contracts yet judged to the same standard.
2. Toxic culture, often easy to get shunted into doing mundane work with little direction or in some cases interaction. Can easily bend over backwards and gain little recognition from some seniors. ‘Sink or swim’ culture where there is often more work than resources and questionable as to who is really benefiting from this way of working.
3. Very hierarchical and political. Some take titles and politics way too far over what wider value they’re creating for the teams they’re managing and their surrounding colleagues.
4. Technology and processes are poor compared to other companies within the financial industry.
5. Promotions feel like who you know rather than what you know and often a popularity contest. If you don’t fit in you’ll notice very quickly and in some cases won’t get a lot of support. A lot of sucking up to senior managers goes on and individuals being prepared to stamp on others to get noticed by seniors, such as snitching and blame culture. Local line managers often left to their own devices which means junior employees struggle to progress. Creates a very toxic environment. Certain personalities dominate and often get the final say on everything.
6. Very hard to climb the ranks, especially if you’re junior and in with a manager who is going to take a lot of persuading that you’re worth it.
7. Flexible working is highly promoted but executed poorly, at the discretion of the line manager which makes the policy very unfair. Rigid 40-hour 9am-6pm week for DBOI contracts from a bygone era with little flexibility around this. An expectation to do overtime whenever required and the ability to only claim in lieu with no financial compensation offered. Some teams have strict rules on when holiday can and can't be used.
8. Some HR staff need serious retraining, some come across as cold, not terribly people-centric and very defensive.
9. Some senior management who get into powerful positions risks becoming blind to the everyday struggles that go on in the front line, including people resigning. There is a ‘management stick together’ culture where some local AVP, VP or D managers are too quick to go on the defensive against their own, their favourites or their seniors which means especially if you’re junior, you will struggle to get listened to even if your argument is perfectly reasonable or at least warrants some concern.

summary: Poor management, unhealthy environment for juniors
advice: There needs to be a cultural shift where managers need to stop viewing employees as just headcount and budget to get things over the line. There is often no real "duty of care" towards individual employees and their careers. The reality of the working environment does not align with the bank's outward projection of its culture and values.
pros:
Annual leave is generous. Work life balance is good. Working locations are great, offices are tidy and comfortable, and flexible remote working is supported. 

Although management is generally poor, there are some very good managers who keep the bank together and deserve credit.

Employee benefits scheme is good (e.g. healthcare). Well-being support in the bank are good, however conflicts with the actual working environment which is generally negative on well-being.
cons:
Since the bank has made a series of cuts over the last few years, a lot of the stronger employees have moved away to pursue other opportunities. This has been seen across all levels. This has left behind a very mixed cohort of employees and managers, and created a stale and unhealthy "every person for themselves" environment out of worry about the risk of further cuts. It has allowed unhealthy office politics to thrive.

Retention of junior talent is very poor, facilitated by a more "selfish" culture. The bank doesn't look after juniors enough and workplace gender diversity is poor. Compensation and benefits are no longer competitive in the industry, so a lot of juniors leave quickly. 

Career progression experience has been primarily negative; good managers who care about individual progression are very rare. It can be difficult to feel valued, depending on culture established by managers in the team. Roles and opportunities also vary extensively in different teams, which makes career progression unbalanced.

It can be more about who can speak the loudest, rather than recognizing talents. For example talented engineers are not as well appreciated as those in more exposed roles who rub shoulders with the right people. Observed a lot of sucking up to managers to get recognized, and it creates a toxic environment.

summary: a melting pot to work in
advice: Listen to people working on the ground and don't make too frequent changes on the roadmap. Accept when things are  not working.
pros: Its a tech friendly place to work in. There are a lot of good people, who are easily approachable and friendly, usually supportive of employees and allows you a good  balance of work and life.
cons: lack of established processess, information sharing especially from management side is lacking, you only get told at the last minute. Sutck to some pre concieved ideas even though there is clear signs that it is not working.

summary: Large organisation can be lots of red tape, but compared to other banks it's best of bad bunch

more work needed to ensure staff are not lost in a world of politics and red tape

summary: Easy job, good salary, not hugely challenging
advice: Implement anonymous 180 reviews on management to gather employee data on their views of their management. Give better training and support to engineers, such as funding Red Hat summits, off-site Azure training, whatever. Measure management by delivery success and not posturing.
pros: Great work-life balance and flexibility, good teams and working environment.

summary: Treausury is great, though a slow and steady environment...
advice: Within Treasury,  move away from a short term way of thinking and restore greater focus on high quality output (not just okay). Short term cost saving measures can already be seen to have negative consequences, especially for staff retention and career progression.
pros:
DB is significantly into executing a strategic overhaul, which is going better than the Street ever expected. Treasury contributed toward this initiative significantly and this is acknowledged across the firm

Treasury has some incredibly smart people who you can learn from

For a department that is traditionally very technical (capital, liquidity, issuance, irbb etc), there is significant focus on soft skills, which is extremely helpful for personal development and enhances saleability when looking for future jobs

It is possible to have a great work life balance. Treasury provides a job for life if so you desire, slow and steady, especially in Frankfurt and more recently London. This comes with its own disadvantages though. Its up to you to push yourself

If joining from externally and you negotiate, salary can be excellent. Benefits are also excellent. Bonuses are OK. Total packages are strong
cons:
Technical excellence seems to be valued below soft skills in the internal value hierarchy. This leads to poor outcomes for a department which by its nature deals in technical topics. 

Part of DB's overhaul includes cost cutting. This has been felt negatively in Treasury and Finance in multiple ways. 

Career progression is possible in the long term but happens at a snails pace for anything other than the more junior levels due to cost pressure. You may find this frustrating, unless you are happy with slow and steady. 

The firm is extremely bureaucratic and slow in some areas. It can be difficult to get things done. Cost pressures mean areas like technology suffer, making it even more difficult to get things done.

Salary rises occur by exceedingly rare exception, mainly for juniors. Salary freezes are frequent for multiple years, even for top performers. Make sure you negotiate the best possible starting salary!

Like many large firms, DB, and TSY in particular, is very far from a meritocracy. Its possible to tick along and receive no medium term outlook difference in ratings appraisals etc against those who strive for excellence. High ratings are also a function of time in the firm in many cases. 

Due to cost pressures, hiring freezes are common. External hires have not been possible in many instances, meaning roles must be filled internally. This can cause issues in deeply technical areas, a brain drain has occurred in Treasury over the past year or two.

summary: Pass the problem & blame culture. Not good flexible working/culture/diversity despite claims.
advice:
Get with the times.

summary: Highly competitive environment: learn a lot but not nice to work for
advice: More respect to employees and clients would benefit. The competitive culture exhausts staff, and in the end those who are able to climb to the top, however smart and outstanding, are those who do not care about the wider ecosystem.
pros:
Quality and intelligence of people
Expertise in wide range of products make it easier to pitch clients
Global reach to be able to answer any question
Powerful brand name
cons: Highly competitive. Company culture is to let people step on others' mandates in order to see who can do best. Of course you are not made aware that someone is trying to do your own job

advice: Review the promotions process at the lower levels and consider promotions throughout the year rather than a rigid once a year program. Do more to weed out poor performers else levels of attrition will remain high whilst good employees leave and the firm is left with poor ones.
pros: Good work life balance and relaxed culture with great colleagues. The main business franchises are well established and strong which promotes a challenging and exciting workplace.
cons: There are barriers to the promotions process to the point where even high performers are being forgotten - ultimately this is stifling incentive. At the same time poor performers are not weeded out.

summary: German Efficiency? Not as efficient as you may expect!
advice: Wake up. The world does not evolve around London and Frankfurt. Value the talent you have and do more to remove barriers that stop people doing their job.
pros: Some very talented people who have the potential to achieve so much more than they are able to here. Birmingham management is good and there are valid attempts to improve culture at least in the Birmingham office.
cons: However, be prepared for endless bureaucracy, office politics, demeaning attitude of London and Frankfurt staff towards people based in non-Hub locations, terrible technology, "we have always done it that way" culture and constant frustration.

advice: Make a massive cut to highly paid, low-zero value MD's which are pooling in upper management. Take some responsibility and take action.
pros: Generally good quality, smart people in front office. Excellent team spirit in the trading group I worked with. Felt like there where common goals everyone was committed to.
cons: Management is poor. A lot of silos and cliques within the company. Management bureaucracy is extremely political and is very much a mediocracy rather than a meritocracy. Early success guarantees a lifetime of employment if you play the political game; thus many managers are promoted to their level of incompetence - the place is riddled with this defect.

advice:
1) There should be one manager, not six. 
2) The manager should be leading and directing, not saying yes to everyone then denying responsibility for their decisions. 
3) A general rule is that one person should not suffer the consequences of another persons mistake, therefore stop low-mid level managers costing people their careers for errors that the managers make.
4) There is a recognised push to deal with the dishonesty and lack of integrity but the managers are not fulfilling this and employees are left with consequences. Example, a manager could make a mistake and blame it on an employee, the employee is then fired. This is simply not acceptable and you absolutely should not allow it to happen in this day and age.
pros:
They pay very well as a salary instead of a bonus.
Their pension contributions are very high, you don't need to contribute yourself.
Work life balance can be ok in some teams.
cons:
1) Horrendous incompetence. It is really apparent from the first day. There are an awful lot of people there who make a lot of mistakes or who just can't do their job. It is great that DB want to keep people, but it really is these long-timers that are holding DB back.

2) Many, many people who all think their job is to micromanage you. This is particularly bad in tech. There are VPs who have no idea what a work item is or what it does or what is needed but have spent years in a job where their role was to find someone else to do the work. As a result, these people will grind projects to a halt.

3) With so many VPs in some teams compared to AVPs, there is a problem similar to the NHS "too posh to wash" problem. If there is six VPs and one AVP, none of them will do any work since they don't want to seem downgraded to AVP. it is absolute nonsense.

4) One day you're told to do one thing, the next you are berated for not knowing someone else decided you should be doing something else. Yes, silly culture.

5) Very old and poor quality software in a lot of teams. This is well known, and often a problem with old systems, but at DB it is horrendously bad and a consequence of the incompetence they are also known for. Their systems make no sense, neither does their code. Their low quality VPs that have been there a very long time and have not kept with the latest technology cause this.

6) An astonishing amount of VP level employees. In some teams there will be just one AVP and six or more VPs. Absolute nonsense. A lot of these VPs will have been around for a very long time and not very good at their job. Their knowledge is out of date and they hold newcomers back from introducing new technology or ideas. This is a problem a lot of companies have, but as usual DB simply doesn't respond.

7) There is air of dishonesty in this company which can be seen by the actions of managers and some VPs, and is a reason for the endless negative media reports surrounding them. They do seem to lack integrity and make decisions with complete disregard for the consequences of those affected. This is simply not how companies operate nowadays. Instead mangers should be accountable, decision makers should be accountable - instead their incompetence affects people directly and causes them to lose their job in some cases. This simply shouldn't be tolerated anymore, other companies sorted out problems like this years ago but DB is just not responding.

summary: Do all the work, deliver but the pay will never catch-up.
advice: Look after the hard workers because they are the people who deliver for you.  Plus break the mode and tear up the rule book....... As you can if you want to.
pros:
One of the top IBs in the world today and have a strong and respected CEO. 
Fast moving and fast paced. 
Leading the way....... Not following.
cons:
A great deal more, for a great dal less. 
They'd rather pay £20k more for an external and pay a £30k search fee to an individual with no network then keep hold of talent and pay them £15k more (per annum).

Take a good look around, really understand the issues. 
See through the fake-ness. 
Assess people on delivery and not on the ability to put a 'spin' on things/talk the talk.

City based.

advice: Make up your mind what this bank is about.
pros: Good benefits. Good place for junior employees who are workhorses really. Some career mobility. Some opportunities to move to front office roles.
cons: No connection between performance and reward. After a certain level in technology they just don’t want to promote you. Rather hire people from outside. Middle management spend more time managing expectations for disappointing compensation then managing talent. Always focused on how they can look good in front of business than understanding why a certain task will take time to deliver. No clue what development involves.

advice: Consider reducing over paid senior managers who don’t work hard. Get rid of offices. Invest in Manager training. Reward hard working junior/middle staff. Bonuses should be paid on ability/effort rather than title. Fix the leaks!
pros: Great benefits, private healthcare for family, 30 days holiday, season ticket loan and more.
cons: No individual bonus or objectives for staff below VP level. Work /life balance poor.  No rewards for hard working junior staff. Hard to get a pay rise or promoted unless you have friends in high places, talent doesn’t matter.

summary: Great reputation and brand, let down by very poor management - frustrating at so many levels.
advice:
Stop promoting your friends, stop all the horse trading that goes on when deciding promotions. Promote only on merit.

Have a flatter structure. Hire better managers. Don't be afraid to sack people who are not performing. Offer training to those you want to keep so that they can actually do the job at hand.

Reward those that do well, and focus on keeping them at the bank. The attrition figures for the high performers are attrocious for a leading bank.
pros: Excellent benefits, friendly workforce, opportunity to work with a variety of people on many different projects, largely due to their outsourcing strategy. Met some really likeable people here.
cons:
Very very very poor management.  They're trying to reorganise the technology division but are just making it worse. Too much management, too many layers. In fact, it often seems that the place is full of managers. Everybody is trying to become AVP, or VP, or Director, or Managing Director, most of the time without merit. People are promoted for the wrong reasons - for length of service and friendships rather than deliverables - definitely NOT a meritocracy.  People are more focussed on promotion and building their own mini-empire rather than delivering well.

They also outsource a lot, and accept work done at a sub-standard level. Most of the management do not understand technology and do not have a handle on quality of work and timelines.  They waste a lot of money on this. Most of the technology staff are sub-standard external consultants. This leads to poor results.

People are also free to choose whatever technology they want to get the job done. There are very few standards.  The people at the top of the technology division need to ask themselves what they are doing and why such basics standards are not in place.

They need qualified people brought in to change things. People with guts to get rid of the mis-firing management, and greater focus to bring in talented developers who will hold the knowledge long after a project has been delivered.

I cannot stress enough how frustrating it is to see layer after layer of middle management.  I do not understand why all the MDs, Directors and VPs are needed, and moreso, what they actually do.   Don't get me wrong, there are some very bright people here at all levels, but they are diluted by really poor employees.

They struggle to keep their best staff for many reasons, and tend to hang on to the people who are performing poorly.  They should look into why this is if they really want to change technology at the bank.

summary: Good micro environment tarnished by poor management, lack of strategy and technological inefficiencies
advice: Please give people the chance to build a career at DB, not somewhere where they will spend a few years before moving on. Often efforts are wasted because of politics
pros: A very diverse working environment, good visibility to other areas and senior management, feels reasonably meritocratic, decent hours

advice: Don't hire someone who has never had experience managing themselves properly or a group of people. Take training and employee development very seriously. Reduce the work hours.

They don't train you first hand instead your development is dependent on manager liking you. Lots  of snitching going on all the time and management cannot be trusted.

advice: Met some people of the higher level management, surprisingly nice people even though I was just an intern they would talk to me for longer than required.

cons: Some desks are less social than others. Lunch is always at the desk rather than having lunch out. Which is more of a banking thing than DB specific I would guess. Just not for everyone.

advice: Offer more competitive salaries and make rotational opportunities more accessible to employees to build up business knowledge in different areas.

summary: A good company to start one's career in Financial Services

pros: Flexible working hours and good benefits. The company is a good place to start one's career.
cons: Moves at a glacial pace due to a lack of change in it's financial position. This dictates constant cost cuts and talent growth can be stifled as a result.  Loyal staff aren't recognized enough.

- global organization w some high performing business lines
- essentially backed by German government i.e. too big to fail in that country
- case study in how not to manage i.e. helpful for any future role

- politics, turnover, lack of cross-functional perspective (and respect) - and total absence of leadership - particularly from managers, seeking to keep jobs

cons: Negative media speculation has shifted focus away from prosperity and introduced uncertainty, despite constant communication and reassurance from management. May be awkward for some to deal with in the short term.

cons: General Morale is poor due to recent comp rounds. Lots of focus on regulation which eats into a lot of your time. Very flow focussed with less and less time spent taking positions

Culture of not making decisions

- Very silo'd

cons: Too political, Meritocracy not rewarded, Poor work life balance.. affects mental health at times with loads of uncertainties, Most people are just used as resources without any future career path

advice: Keep supporting junior staff. Start paying at par with market to retain talent. Remove super process orientation mindset. Avoid org restructuring very few months.

cons: Can be very process oriented and sometimes too bureaucratic. Pay can be below the market for existing employees. Related departments operate in silos but this is changing.

advice: Keep on investing in IT especially around internal processes softwares and communication. Improve front office functions workstreams to increase efficiency.
pros: Obviously team specific but overall good atmosphere across the bank with challenge driven people that respect work life balance.
cons:
Typical investment banking downsides (esp. long hours) 
A lot could be improved regarding IT: increasing middle office processes transferred to front office teams due to cost saving plans, inefficient softwares, communication and internal processes across different product teams could really be improved as well.

advice: Review the promotions guidelines to ensure good staff are not overlooked and lost to competitors. Stop internal marketing to employees as this is a complete waste of money.
pros: Good work life balance, if you are able to manage your manager and not be overloaded! Good support with learning, courses etc. Good remuneration and benefits.
cons: Very slow for change to happen. Too many committees, meetings etc. They waste money on branding exercises within the company. Promotions are not handled fairly
