advice: To change your culture, fire the incompetent and hire some people who know what they're doing.
pros: Some good people, if you get the right kind of boss you can work on a pet project for a while and then quit before anyone notices you haven't delivered anything really usable.
cons: so, so many - most of the MDs and Ds here would absolutely not be hired at any other bank because they have zero skills, so they're clinging on until they go down with the ship.

summary: Hiring race horses to plough the fields.
advice: Clear lines of accountability needed. Holding mgt both junior and senior clearly accountable for explicit and measurable deliverables.
pros: Excellent packages,  great opportunities for graduates with wish to explore overseas roles, huge amount of improvement opportunities. Hiring strategy strong with great talent pool.
cons: Considerable imbalance in male/female population at snr levels. Passive aggressive culture making it extremely hard to roll out significant change.

advice: More opportunities for loyal employees are needed...
pros:
If you're after stability, Db will give that to you.
Also great location for family - if you want to get away from London
cons: As there isn't much other investment banking companies in Birmingham you will find it hard to negotiate salaries etc and will probably have to stay out unless you're willing to move location.

summary: Focus Is on the wrong things
advice: Treat and value your staff better and snap out of this "political game' mentality
pros: Good location in Birmingham
cons:
Internal campaigns are embarrassing 
Diversity is good if senior managers understand it
Senior managers are poor role models
Senior managers are mostly political
Talented hard working Employees should be valued higher than the social worker who attends events

summary: Good pay, but do your research
pros: Good pay and general benefits. Multiple offices located across serval countries with lots of roles available to choose from for those in the right positions.
cons: Very hierarchical, difficult to progress unless you befriend the right individuals. Generally required to stay in roles for minimum amount of time (circa 18 months plus) before being allowed or supported in onwards rotations. Work life balance poor.

advice: Deliver what CEO has given as vision. CEO should get IT savvy NED to validate promise of COO.
pros: I am lucky to have a manager that gets it and many of my colleagues are great too. Change has started and new NFR lead will hopefully energise.
cons: So much needs fixing and belt tightening makes investment difficult.  Communication between silos is poor and org structure is overly complex.

summary: Good employer for a junior employee
advice: Implement change at a smaller level as opposed to trying to change the entire bank at once.
pros: The graduate program is very thorough and offers varied job rotations and qualification opportunities. Also being a global investment bank means there are options to move abroad internally and are often encouraged by senior management.
cons: Being a large bank can mean that any change initiatives being undertaken can be very slow and sometimes ineffective which can damage employee morale with large sums of money being wasted.

advice: Recognize people who let their accomplishments do the talk and not those who just talk.
pros: Good work/life balance for an investment bank, good place to learn, very good benefits (especially pension contributions), located in the City.
cons: Lots of office politics, bureaucracy and corporate spin. Show more important than quality of your work, very slim chances of getting promoted if you don't play the game well. Ensure you get a very good base pay and adequate corporate title when joining.

pros: Good central location in city centre for transport.  Many cons but morale is OK in some of the teams , this varies from area to area.
cons: Local snr management very political. Compared to London salary progression much slower, promotions much slower, benefits much poorer although work is the same and both locations judged to the same standards.  When speaking to recruiters  when looking to move the much lower Birmingham salary will impact your future earning potential for several years.

advice:
I really appreciate the help and advice provided by my manager in terms of how to work efficiently. 
more introduction of the management structure to new employees could be better.
pros: DB has exceptional training program. It provides professional and friendly working environment.  It also provide opportunities for employees to try different roles within the company
cons: lunch from DB's restaurant is awful. Trying to arrange most or all division within one big building instead of separates one may improve the branding of DB in London.

summary: (For London) - Not a company I would recommend
advice:
Listen to what your employees have to say and give them a voice.
Empower your employees to make their own decisions without fear of retribution
pros:
Salaries, bonus and learning and development opportunities are good.
Global organisation which opens up  a range of job opportunities across the world
cons:
A completely non-collaborative approach between senior management and staff - everything is top down
People managed purely through performance not through behaviours -leading to a fear culture
Exceedingly long hours
No reward and recognition programs
No clear strategy

summary: A shadow of the institution's former self
advice: Continue re-staffing the (senior) management layer and win back trust and motivation of employees other than with compensation
pros:
- International & fast-paced environment
- Compensation
- Lots of smart people with different academic and professional background
cons:
- Strategic direction unclear for years
- Senior management doesn't practice what it preaches (lack of role models)
- Bank is in ongoing "clear-up" mode over scandals and investigations, focus on innovation and business development significantly reduced
- Challenges in corporate culture, e.g. decision-making and people management

advice: Company has lost its way. Several years of declining share price to 8 euros highlights this. Appreciate the staff you have rather than constantly hiring externally all the time
pros: Good benefits and flexible work life balance. Lots of opportunities to rotate to different roles
cons: Very difficult to ever get a payrise these days. I know people who have not had any movement in comp for several years. Promotion is also difficult and sadly if you dont know the right people you wont move far

summary: Good work/life balance but choose another bank if you are junior.
advice:
Improve compensation/recognition for junior staff as many are leaving/have left for competitors and it seems no one really cares?
Reduce bureaucracy.
pros:
Work/life balance is better than peers.
Diverse workforce.
cons:
Base salary for junior staff is on par with the market when joining however increasingly lags behind the market each year. Forget about bonus. Unfortunately losing a lot of talent to competitors.
Way too much bureaucracy.
Senior management talk about a lot over the past 5+ years but the evidence is yet to be seen.

advice: Walk the talk when it comes to being a true meritocracy and have the courage to fire senior mangers with 80s attitudes who  empire build by favouring those who support them personally rather than those who are best for the Bank at their jobs.
pros: Good Employee benefits and some very good people to work with.
cons:
Some 80s style mangers and attitudes still prevail in London despite the corporate hype stated.
If you are in Operations, beware of Offshoring your job to subsdiuaries in Birmingham or Bangalore

advice: Effort should be taken to improve a sense of purpose for junior employees. Perhaps give them for freedom in creating their own solutions and truly listening to their suggestions.
pros:
Good hours
Nice salary (fixed pay increased and bonus decreased)
Good perks, including museum passes, CFA sponsorship, internal training courses, etc.
Access to senior management, including head of division
cons:
Bureaucracy
Inefficiency
Most of all, as an analyst, you do not see clearly how you can add value to the firm, which can be discouraging and uninspiring.

summary: Exciting workplace with excellent work and employer ethic
pros: Great people working on exciting projects. But what I appreciate the most is the Corporate Social responsibility...and especially that the bank does not shout it out loud to gain brownie points. It just does it quietly. I never knew how much Deutsche Bank does for the communities. Paid volunteer days, donation matching, community projects, cultural and social sponsorships, and, and, and...just amazing.
cons: So far I see no Deutsche Bank specific cons. Well, it is a financial institution in a troubled financial market. But the effects for my job are rather on the pros as it makes the daily job extremely challenging and exciting.

summary: Typical European bank - lots of bureaucracy, can be painful to get things done
advice: It's understandable that technology goals might not align with short term business goals from the desk, but when this is completely skewed one way, the business relationship suffers and puts desk facing front office teams often in difficult situations.
pros: Some reasonably strong senior developers, the banks's size means it can invest in infrastructure and areas that smaller shops can't
cons: Plenty of mediocre people around across all levels.  Lots of red tape and processes to get anything done, within Technology, the focus was on pleasing tech management rather than delivering projects for the desk.

summary: Review of Trading role at Deutsche Bank
pros:
The work in credit trading is quite interesting. In structured products, you will face new challenges and the product offering to the client, hedging strategy will need to be customized and brainstormed time to time.
Flow trading will require being thorough with the markets and need developing intelligent views on the market. One needs to be smart and proactive in hedging and rebalancing the book which is where you can make the difference to meet your year-end targets.
cons:
Increasing regulatory prudence, increased capital requirements, limited risk appetite which limits the opportunites for the banks.
Hence I have a neutral outlook for future for the investment banking.

summary: Extremely unbearable recruitment as a world known company
pros: Nice working place in city London
cons:
This company withdrew the offer after:
1. formal congrats email from the head
2. asking for personal information e.g. passport, home address, sending confidential material of the company (benefits etc.)
3. confirmation to the candidates that they can reject all other offers, and they did

Because HR asked the salary provided by another company that offered me a position, once I knew about it, I told the HR in an email. This became the reason why they decided to withdraw the offer. "Your words about salary are against our values". No official letter or explanation. HR and the business unit worked totally separately with no coherence.

From my point of view, this bank, and its in-house consulting unit, do not know about their own values and how to carry them on.

advice: Nothing specific - I thought teams were well led and we had a very influential and charismatic leader.  Felt I was given plenty of opportunity to succeed.
pros: Travel opportunities for this role were great - very professional team to work with.  Learned many new skills and had opportunity to work with some really brilliant colleagues.  Started as a maternity cover which resulted in a permanent hire.
cons: Long hours however the team I worked with were very cohesive and supportive.  Went through a technical upgrade in the candidate management system which made the first year a bit tricky.

summary: Senior Leaders are making kinder garden decisions
advice: Don't recruit very senior people from Goldman Sachs. Since they joined the bank has not done well but the people concerned still got paid well.
pros: Their pension scheme is good
cons: The more senior people are winging it. Hence, why the bank is self emploding in my opinion. For years they let highly paid individuals flourish without having adequate controls in place. In my opinion their controls are still poor. So be aware. They also paid poor redundancy packages to individuals who were loyal to them during the last horrible 12 years of fine after fine after fine.

summary: Long work hours is a problem.
advice: NA
pros: Usually employ earns good salary and they have good benefit package. Office is new and modern in Canary warf and you can work in good environment.
cons: Long work hours. I often had to work until midnight during week days and work on weekends.   Sometimes I had to work from very early in the morning due to the time difference of other countries.

advice: Try spending more time on the trading floor to get better understanding of the business you are in. Turning up before 11am sometimes might be helpful as well.
pros: Opportunity to travel,  large database of interesting trade ideas and investment ideas, some people are quite intelligent
cons: EXTREMELY POOR CULTURE, people are very unwilling to help, massive backstabbers. Management on the other hand is completely clueless as to what is going on in the bank. Systems are very poor and inefficient, getting trades done is close to impossible due to internal inefficiencies. Also sales people are not at all cooperative.

summary: Very impressive workforce: capable and passionate.  Great organisation to grow, compete and develop in.
advice: Compete harder
pros: Good opportunities to those who work hard.  Well paid but narrowing.  Get great experience in financial services and management.  Global perspective.  Virtual teams.
cons: You can't coast; you need to keep adding value.  Competition can be harsh and unfair to career development.  Not suitable for shrinking violets.

summary: Great place to learn and grow, challenging but full of very smart people that make it fun
advice: Focus on system rationalization, data and project management skills throughout the organization as fundamental core strategy enabler with tangible annual targets and measurable outcomes
pros: Loads of opportunities, quick progression possible when you deliver, loads of smart people, lots to learn all the time, strong employees networks and outside work interest for those interested , feeling of belonging
cons: Too much admin, slow decision making, cost pressure which to some extent inhibit collaboration to get issues solved, still unclear whether we have a credible party to great financial performance again

advice: More transparent communications between high level management and low level employee. Thinking about the benefits of the whole company rather than personal benefits.
pros:
Big company, good benefits. Work from home. Smart colleagues and good team work spirit.
There are a lot of Intenal mobility opportunities.
cons: Long hours work. Performance is not rewarded. Difficult to get promotion and pay rise. Some common problems of big company, complicated hierarchy.

advice: In the preparing for maternity leave workshop we were told that DB recognises and strives to retain talent, yet on returning from my second maternity leave, I was told that part-time non-travelling role was not possible. I asked what other opportunities there were in the bank and I was advised the best option would be for me to leave and secure a part-time role elsewhere.
pros:
Good opportunities with interesting people
Opportunity for development
cons:
Bit of a clique atmosphere - if your face doesn't fit
When I asked for a part-time role, I was told I would be better off leaving

summary: Good place to work to keep life and work balance
advice:
1) Less bureaucracy. Very often an easy change request (i.e. add the drop down value) takes months to execute!
2) more engagement of ordinary employees into the decision making
3) more support of automation of the processes and getting rid of manual work where applicable
pros:
1) Nice location
2) Possibility to take part in different courses and trainings 
3) Good work-life balance
cons: A lot of bureaucracy, lack of dependecy management between departments, very difficult to see the whole picture, little bonus and salary increase every year, management is reluctant to promote you

advice: There are too many layers of management and this often means that decision making takes a lot longer than needed
pros: There's a great work life balance and plenty of opportunity for career progression. Also the employee benefits are very good.
cons: I honestly cannot think of any cons. I have worked for the bank for over 5 years now and have no reason for looking elsewhere

summary: Work life balance good - slow career, bank is not profitable for years which is reflected in the bonus and salary growth
pros: Work life balance good - relaxed environment, job security (until a certain level of seniority beyond which there is none)
cons: Growth / career opportunities are slow - highly bureaucratic organisation - slow in moving forward due to complex and rigid processes

advice: Carry on doing what you're doing, I think the Bank is moving in the right direction under the current leadership team.
pros: I've been with the bank nearly 4 years and have found career progression, mobility and colleagues to be the top positives aspects. If you can work hard and show it then the sky is the limit.
cons: Some of the systems can be frustrating.

advice: Retain talent by benchmarking salaries against the market on a regular basis. Continue to offer volunteering and fundraising opportunities
pros: Lots of training and support opportunities. The Bank supports employees with time off for volunteering and raising money for charity.
cons: Salary does not rise in line with market. This means after a few years of employment, you are earning below the market rate.

advice: Cost cutting should apply to the right areas - not make generating sustainable revenue harder. You need to concentrate on removing excessive middle management.
pros: Generally good benefits and offers a significant challenge. Name can still be good on CV, albeit work to do. That’s all
cons: Do not tend to reward longstanding staff or recognise potential. Has fostered a significant political environment, especially in middle management.

advice: Continue to lead with austerity and promote cultures that that are all inclusive to promote the the brand of DB.
pros: Good environment where colleagues are held accountable. Access to career progression and support structures. Good central location of offices which helps.
cons: Poor infrastructure functions who are not kept to the higest standards, long hours with pay reward not reflecting. Not that bad though.

summary: Deutsche Bank Technology; Needs more work
advice:
Foster a culture of innovation (not just lip service)
Establish framework to develop and promote 'home grown' talent. Tendency to outsource, rather than leverage existing talent pool
pros:
Generous employee benefits, especially pension contributions
Good work life balance
cons:
Poor career progression
Too hierarchical/bureaucratic
Too IT Vendor/Contractor heavy; no real definitive culture
No clear defined strategy. Too much focus on cost-cutting

summary: Constantly changing structures ensures nothing actually gets finished
pros: Good, competitive pay and great benefits. Decent career progression if you work hard and actively seek it. Given a lot of responsibility and autonomy from day one.
cons: Management structures change seemingly daily with no real purpose, clarity, focus, or ultimate goal laid out before the changes are made. As such the work seems aimless and the intentions of the reorgs are 'retro-fitted' to meet personal agendas.

advice: See the value in flexible working and part time. Missing out/losing good talent because of a prescriptive old fashioned way of working.
pros: Great employee benefits, exciting to be part of a large global employer. Very professional colleagues. People on top of their game. Great development opportunities.
cons: Not great for flexible working. Face time is a real issue. Long hours and an old fashioned way of working.

pros: not much pressure, work life balance, international exposure, everyone is very approachable, friendly people, flat kind of work environment, a lot of freedom is given and there is hardly any kind of micro management
cons: When you are working at the junior level, senior level people do not take much interest in your career and hence at times at junior level, you are very unsure and frustrated about your career path.

advice: Senior management should clearly sponsor cross-function programmes and deputise so that sponsorship traction is not lost if management departs the bank or business area.
pros: Opportunity for exposure to every facet of investment bank business
cons: Limited cross-function cooperation as budgets are allocated to siloed programmes of work rather than across horizontal domains that span business areas.  Churn of senior management means accountability is lost year to year, leaving sponsorship vacuums.

pros:
Promote flexible working.
Generous maternity and healthcare package.
cons:
Morale is low. High level of attrition especially in offshore locations.

Becoming more German-centric. 

Inequality between the way that the Germany-based staff are treated vs the Rest of the World.

Top performers were part of the retained organisation but are now being short changed when it comes to redundancy. Loyalty and good performance clearly do not pay.

summary: Great place if you work hard and build strong networks
advice: Find hidden gems and promote them. Get rid of non contributors.
pros:
Good mentoring and management support available if you are pro active.

Investing in new products and new technology.

Lots of opportunities to contribute and grow.

Career progression if you show your talent and go out of your way.
cons:
Too many non-contributors in management roles.

Visibility required to move up.

advice: Management in technology tends to follow  cronyism model and in many cases there are people and role that do not bring benefits but stay in place due to connections.  Too many applications and people supporting them and reluctance for change.
pros: Generous benefit scheme and holiday allowance and in general good working conditions.
cons: Not very good salary prospect after graduate program, yearly increase only aligns with inflation.

pros: Big global bank;  presence with clients is good; some good opportunities available;  high aspirations
cons: Highly political;  Need to be connected to the right people or left behind (ie inconsistent application of performance expectations);  Suffers from lack of confidence in own grown people and always seems to look outside instead of growing from within;  very poor track record supporting women in front office positions

advice: slim down managerial/committee culture to enable faster, nimble decision making. Focus on core, profitable businesses and review productivity/input of infrastructure functions to find possible cuts
pros: truly global bulge bracket allowing exposure to a wide variety of businesses and cultures. Decent graduate programme allowing new recruits to hit the ground running.
cons: Significant bureaucracy with several committees and layers of management, below market pay, poor systems and processes that are never addressed sufficiently

summary: Company is financial trouble, low/no bonuses and limited salary increase in last 4 years
advice: - Maintain good communication with the Senior Management,   follow the 'old rules', be agreeable
pros: Some excellent people work there. You can make friends in the office.
cons:
- Outdated technology and processes,
- The culture of 'escalations'. Too much finger pointing and lack of a team ownership
- Poor communication between teams,
- Extremely difficult to implement any changes

summary: Great working experience, great career starter
advice: Embrace the workforce more, do not treat them like they are there solely for the benefit of the firm. Work hand in hand with achieving goals
pros:
Fantastic opportunity for people looking for a first job or an entry level job
Brand New multi-million pound HQ in Birmingham
Great work-life balance 
Small and efficient teams 
Great training programs
cons:
Lack of transparency with senior management 
Personal growth within the bank is extremely difficult and borderline unfair
Cliquey working environment

jobTitle: Associate FIG Capital Markets and Treasury Solutions
summary: Market leading bank in FIG capital markets with a lot of institutional issues to solve.
advice: Come up with a credible strategy, improve overall quality of management, reward people better for their efforts.
pros: Market leading, fixed income powerhouse that tops league tables for FIG capital markets business. Quality of people in DCM/ECM across coverage, syndicate, etc is very high.
cons: Politics, politics, politics. People continuously being squeezed: achieve more with less for less compensation every year. Career progression not based on merit.

advice: The risk and reward structure is out of balance for employees and this needs to be reviewed urgently. There is too much complexity built in by middle management and this needs to be addressed in order to reduce the cost pressures on the organisation.
pros:
A solid client base who love DB's excellent client service.

Entrepreneurial spirit is encouraged.
cons:
No sense of personal accountability at middle management level.

Too much complexity built in the organisational processes.

summary: Reactive non-strategic culture with high caliber people
pros: My colleagues were very smart and capable. High caliber of staff. The Bank pays higher base salaries on average than most of their competitors.  Hours are reasonable for IB.
cons: Non-strategic culture where Senior Management react to new developments in a scatter-brained manner  and change direction daily. Working here felt like a knee-jerk reaction roller coaster. Poor culture for women and limited career prospects  for non-revenue generating support VP/D level staff.

advice: Find better ways to motivate the workforce and give employees of all levels the opportunity to be heard.
pros: Decent pay and bonuses (although not exceptional)
cons: Poor communication from senior leaders (although there have been major organisation/personnel changes since I left in 2015). Bright, talented staff in my department felt unheard and frustrated. Lack of opportunity to move roles internally. Very hierarchical and a lot of "dead wood" employees coasting and not adding value.

jobTitle: Vice President Head of Release & Environments Management
summary: Not the best firm on the street
advice: If you spent half as much time working with each other instead of playing games, DB wouldn’t be in the mess it’s in
pros: Dedicated people, trying to do good jobs and what's right. Some real industry SMEs that are willing to educate & help
cons: DB used to have an identity - it doesn’t any more. Very little direction from the top, and way too much politics to get things done efficiently.

advice: When senior management make decisions that will effect teams within the bank, it would be useful for them to get view points of those working within the teams, as it will directly effect them,
pros: Good work life balance, great learning opportunites, intelligent staff, academics, good trading house, strong IB arm, strong corporate responsibility, global bank
cons: There is never enough compensation for the junior staff at DB, sometimes there is a lack of recognition from senior management`

summary: Pleasant place to work, nice people, interesting projects, good hours
pros: It is a pleasant place to work, the people are friendly and generally competent, the projects I have worked on have been interesting and a good learning curve, the hours are good
cons: Current economic climate put people of their toes, a lot of protectionism for projects that are not necessarily the best strategic platform for the bank but have a lot of built up skill

summary: Positive experience, have been able to learn, progress within roles and taken opportunities to move into new roles.
pros: Ability to be involved in change the bank and run the bank processes, multiple divisions represented and opportunities for progression.
cons: Perceived reliance on London for direction and decision making. Constant bad press affecting morale. Looks like operations / back office taking the hit in terms of compensation despite praise for efforts in keeping the bank on track through litigation.

summary: I have had a generally positive experience, opportunities to move across departments and roles to meet my career goals
pros: I like that the company is big on voluntary work and giving back to the community. They support work life balance by allowing work from home days. Maternity and pension pay is among the best in the industry.
cons: At the moment the company is not in the news for positive achievements. This can be a dampener on morale.

pros: Great pay, flexible hours, DB has its own nursery, additional pension contribution, company car, bicycle to work, private health insurance with 100% bill cover, MyFlex, gym, meals included, taxi paid, business class flights
cons: lack of discipline, Frankfurt management promotes own people

pros:
- Culture and work life balance.
- Opportunity to work on interesting problems.
cons:
- Complex management hierarchy, makes the decision making process convoluted.
- Not well taught of business strategies.
- Staff are sometimes undervalued and appreciated.
- Constant changes in management, makes it difficult to follow through on objectives as things tend to "chop and change" a lot.
- Specific personalities tend to dominate.

advice: Stop seeing staff as easily replaceable and do something about the high turnover rate. Start caring more for employees and their wellbeing instead
pros: Great insight into financial crime and good stepping stone, able to leave at bang on 5 every day as long as you start on time, flexible hours (to a certain extent)
cons: Never any bonuses, minimal pay rises, lack of progression, terrible managers who care more about stats and their own power than their team’s wellbeing, lack of appreciation, far too much team politics, even within management

advice: Be more open about cost cutting measures
pros: The pay is generally in the top quartile. They encourage mobility globally to support career advancement. Do not generally expect you to work 12 hour a day in IT.
cons: A person is expected to handle several roles - less scope to focus on a particular technology or project.

summary: Salaries are low compare with other banks
advice: Senior management should make sure that their objectives are propagated down
pros: The bank put a big effort on employee developments, help to charities, good sponsor on art activities
cons: It is not very visible what to do to grow with the bank and lack of motivation coming from Senior Management

summary: Good company and work life balance
advice: Allow for more structured global mobility for employees who want to move into other areas.
pros: Worked in IT as project manager. Work is relatively not stressful and allow for good work life balance.
cons: Work may not be too challenging and becomes boring after a year or two. Not much career progression especially in the middle to back office.

advice: Keep going with the turnaround plans
pros: Interesting challenges at a global player in financial markets which is beginning to turn a corner after a tough few years. Good leadership.
cons: Still a large reliance on external/contract workers in technology - the perm proposition isn't quite compelling enough. Plenty of waste still needs cutting out of the organisation

summary: interesting place to just "turn the handle" on a daily basis
advice: Managers need training to manage. Give credit where it's due.
pros:
Interesting work at times.
Most of the people were good to work with.
cons: This is a large place, and to have a general downside would be unfair, but from the perspective of one area, achievements were not recognised. Recognition was misplaced.

advice:
Hire more people in IT
Fund it by firing more middle management
pros:
Working hours are reasonable compared to other IBs
Vast majority of colleagues are talented and friendly people
New management appears to have a more coherent direction
cons:
Poor salary and bonus structure - disincentivises going 'above and beyond'
Outdated system architecture - regulatory/Brexit pressures are preventing critical process improvement initiatives

advice:
Review your layers of management
Enable and encourage people to make decisions
pros:
Working remotely made easy through technology that works quite seamlessly.
Colleagues are by and far the most responsive and helpful I have encountered in The City
cons: Given its recent trials and tribulations, it is very bureaucratic, with layers of governance and internal politics to match

summary: Dump. Some great people let down by poor top down management. Work elsewhere if you can.
pros:
Salary is okay, but other banks pay more
Canteen okay
Some great benefits such as share options which are used to lure you in.
cons:
HR are a miserable and can be aggressive. I got to see this because I asked for a few improvements which virtually all other banks had (multi-faith rooms etc)
Good staff and line manager can be found but ruined by everything else.
Poor facilities, gym overcrowded (if you can get a place in the first place)

summary: you will be kept on your toes
pros: Well known global brand.  Global mobiliity and opportunities to move within the company are not just spoken about but real and smooth and fluid.  Good vacation package and great internal infrastructure.
cons: Friendly and genuine people, however backstabbing is normal so expect colours of flags to change with the daily tides

advice: Need to look at bringing salary in line, there is a very big pay gap when newly appointed AVP's are earning higher than long established VP's
pros: Excellent benefits package which you can pick and choose, Pension contribution is 12.5%
cons: Low pay package in comparison both internally and externally, not very good at utilising benchmark.

advice: Recognise and reward excellence to ensure retention of top talent.
pros: Great culture and great people, DB is certainly an employer of choice for the region and attracts some of the best talent there is.
cons: Highly political and is being influenced more and more by German/EU regulators, but no different than any bank and their primary/home regulators.

summary: Good work life balance but you feel lost
advice: Do not invest in the new technology for sake of investing and also do not simply drop the project without knowing its impact in the name of cost cutting. Management team should meet junior employees to motivate them instead of only meeting direct reportees.
pros:
Work life balance
Good salary and benefits
cons:
Old technology
Hierarchy
Feel lost
No long time vision

advice: I hope that current senior management is able to rekindle some of their forebears' success, and knack for good business.
pros: I left Deutsche Bank in 2009 to pursue a  new career. During my years at the bank, it was the most amazing place to work. Challenging, entrepreneurial and intellectual.
cons: There were none during my period at the bank.

advice: Management tend to be more side tracked on their achievements rather than support the team in bringing out the best in them.
pros: Good people to Work with. Opportunity available for the right candidate
cons: Takes a while to move up. They operate a bell curve process which puts a lot of strain on organisation wide morale

advice: Sorry, it's no easy job to turn this one around - no good advice.
pros: Good pensions and benefits system. Chance of rapid career progression when senior people are let go. Decent base salaries, but bonuses are low.
cons: Weak outlook for the future, increasing work load as redundancies are made, poor staff morale, archaic IT systems, aversion to risk taking/making money.

advice: Put more emphasis on people leaders as a role. Too often managers are too focussed on their own deliveries and growth and not focussed enough on their teams.
pros: Some good benefits and a lot of good people to work with.
cons: Extremely disappointing rewards and a lack of a feeling of employees being valued.

summary: Been through a rough spell, things are looking up
advice: Remove the multiple layers of MD/D's and bureaucracy.

summary: Appalling place to work if you're in technology
advice:
This advice is to senior management - GET RID OF ALL THE LEVELS OF VPs! You're looking to cut costs, there's 90k per person right there!
Invest in IT if you want to be a leading/cutting edge company. The company I now work for has a healthy budget, no unneccessary managers, values a meritorious culture, and is the world leader in its industry. There's food for thought!
pros: some decent honest people, great place to work if you like to backstab, play the game and use a lot of jargon in your day-to-day life
cons:
Where to begin - please note this is based on working in IT Infrastructure (London office) and so may not be typical of the company as a whole, only my experience of it in this area:

- a culture of long hours where they aren't required! Sure we all have times when we have to stay late, or even want to stay to finish off that project or meet that deadline. But here people consciously stay at their desks and chat, go on facebook, make personal calls etc, until 8-9pm, then make a show of sighing and leaving, and come in the next morning (often around 10am due to their 'late night') and tell everyone how they never left until 9pm. And they actually gain promotion on the basis of this!! 

- constantly driving down costs and reducing teams who do all the work, resulting in teams of 1 or 2 running entire regions, all the while keeping multiple layers of management. As an example, you can have 2 people reporting to a VP, reporting to another VP, reporting to a D, reporting to another D, reporting to an MD, reporting to another MD before you advance to any real level in the company. The amount of money being saved is completely negated by a completely unnecessary hierarchy

- completely sexist - no women advance in this area unless they 'look good'. Those who don't have to work hard but never advance

- advancement based on friendships and contacts rather than achievement and potential

- no clear focus of where they are headed - the same projects and improvements cycle every few years justifying projects and looking to change and improve standards with no real intention to do so

- offices falling apart and drive towards 'clear desk policy' whereby all staff work on a stark white open desk with no privacy walls, and have to put all desk and personal items in a locker (no pedastals allowed under desks) result in offices with all the charm and personality of a hospital

- the lowest morale of any company I have worked in (over 20 years City/finance experience)

- the new CEOs came on board with the amazing idea of reducing Infrastructure by 60%. I know they're not sexy like the traders, but they keep the rest of you running! Don't forget that! 

- more of an opinion this one, but every single person I encounter where the subject of DB comes up has some sort of bad story - "I know someone who worked there who had a nervous breakdown", "aren't they a terrible company to work for", "I've heard they're bad". Now as I say, this is opinion, but I've never had this for any other place I've worked, and as mentioned above I have 20+ yrs of corporations

And this is all that immediately comes to mind. I'm sure if I had a think I could find a lot more!

summary: Toxic work atmosphere, understaffed teams, and inexperienced leadership
advice:
I would suggest that management pay close attention to the departments experiencing high turnover rates and take the time to understand the underlying causes. It would be beneficial to assess the management practices in these areas, as they may be contributing to the loss of valuable, highly skilled employees or the unnecessary dismissal of staff. 

I also recommend considering the hiring of additional personnel to reduce burnout and promote a healthier work-life balance for current employees. Furthermore, updating the existing systems and processes with automation could significantly improve efficiency and ease the workflow. 

Lastly, providing leadership and influence training for management could help improve team dynamics and retention, ensuring a more supportive and productive work environment.
pros: Competitive salary and a prime office location, offering easy accessibility.
cons:
The leadership lacks the necessary qualifications, often making strategic decisions that are ultimately discarded, leading to wasted effort and inefficiency. The HR department fails to address serious workplace issues, such as bullying and harassment, and frequently turns a blind eye to these problems. As a result, many employees leave the organization within a year or two. 

Additionally, a shortage of staff forces employees to work late hours and weekends, often handling the workload of three to four people.

advice: Deutsche Bank lacks proper training for new employees on product offerings and policies. Hiring a dedicated trainer would help equip new hires with the knowledge needed to effectively represent the bank, build market presence, and drive valuable business growth. One manager has been with the bank for 17 years and still lacks proper product knowledge, raising concerns about how management expects him to effectively train subordinates on the bank's offerings and policies. This lack of effective training and guidance is a key reason behind the high attrition rate, with employees leaving the company within 6-8 months.
pros: Deutsche Bank offers a competitive salary at the Sales Manager level, often exceeding that of leading Indian brands like HDFC, Kotak, or ICICI. The bank also provides attractive incentives, albeit with caps, which are highly rewarding for those who perform well.

pros: The Jacksonville building at 5201 Gate Parkway is really nice and well kept. They do have a hybrid work location and up until 2024 it was 2 days in office and 3 WFH. This is a global bank, so the opportunities to move around, within Jacksonville, within the US and throughout the globe are there if you know where to look and how to market yourself.
cons: In the past couple of years (and from what I heard from employees there longer than I was) the annual increases are almost non existent and where they are given to certain people it is not publicly known why. Additionally, like other financial institutions, who you know can make and or break your career and DB is no exception. They frequently change direction in terms of the overall goals for the organization and even your department but rarely if ever fully explain why, so employees are left wondering if the changes made are well thought out. In terms of infrastructure technology wise, it can use a makeover as a lot of systems are antiquated. Compared to other banks I have worked at this one would be middle of the road. Not exactly the worst, but not exactly the best either. Be aware that in most cases you will be working among peers who could potentially manage you from another country or timezone as they love spaghetti and matrix organizations. It sometimes feels that it is to give certain people titles and responsibilities (like being the head of a global function) when in reality they aren't head of anything or leading much less on a day to day basis.In terms of the worst scenarios is when dealing with layoffs. I know that sometimes they happen but when it is done the staff are actually told that they should not tell anyone else about them being laid off and sometimes there is no rhyme or reason. Some are being laid off and walked out same day, some are being given a month or more longer to find a job, then collect severance. For the people left in the building they wonder of course if they are next and the stress level is ultra high. None of it is pleasant but I think they can handle it better.

summary: Working at DB did not meet my expectations...
advice:
- Create standards for people managers. It's basically the luck of the draw as to whether you get a manager that can effectively manage their team, or one that will put their own ambitions ahead of their direct reports.
- Provide better training. Shadowing and online courses are not good enough.
- Make the promotion process more transparent.
- Treat employees like they are human and not just a number. Show us that we are valued as we do the actual work that helps you meet your bottom line.
- Rent an actual venue for the end-of-the-year party instead of leaving your employees to freeze in the back parking lot.
pros:
- The benefits and time off are good, especially the health insurance and maternity leave.
- Main building in Jax has cafe, gym, and nurse's office, and is in a great location.
- Most people that work there are friendly and approachable.
- There are a lot of resource groups, and ways to get involved and meet people outside of your team.
cons:
- The pay is not the greatest. What you come in with, you will be at for a while. You basically have to promote in order to get a raise.
- The promotions seem to be more political or based on favoritism, rather than merit and hard work.
- Because of this, management is not typically as knowledgeable as they could be, and a lot of the job is up to the associates to figure it out.
- Training is nonexistent for most roles. It's a sink or swim culture. 
- They have done some upgrades to the systems, but they are still slow.
- They changed the hybrid schedule to a required 3 days a week, with barely 90 days' notice, to start in the summer when school is out. This is a huge inconvenience for employees, especially those that need to figure out childcare.
- Morale is definitely low amongst a lot of associates. It has become very production and metrics driven, and some people have been laid off. I have heard multiple stories of employees being called out on team calls for not meeting metrics that are sometimes unreasonable. Your work-life balance is sometimes compromised in order to hit the numbers.

pros:
Nestled within the walls of our historic office building lies a tale of two climates. On the ground, a rich tapestry of well-aged carpets tells stories of bygone eras, except on the third floor. Here, in the rarefied air of the CEO’s sanctum, the carpet is as fresh and plush as the ideas purportedly birthed above it.

Winter within these walls adheres to a strict, brisk 19 degrees - a policy not without its charm, encouraging a camaraderie born of shared shivers and hot beverage runs. However, come summer, the building embarks on a tropical transformation. Temperatures soar to a balmy 28 degrees, a reminder that not all saunas require membership. This naturalistic approach to climate control ensures that, regardless of season, the environment remains a topic of warm (or cool) discussion.

This office is not merely a place of work; it’s a test of survival, where the fittest (or most acclimatized) can thrive. It’s a world where the third floor boasts not only the best views but the newest carpet, marking a lush, green oasis in an otherwise challenging climate. Here, every floor tells a story, every season brings a new adventure, and the true spirit of the office comes not from the temperature but the warmth of its people.
cons:
In an intriguing twist of office lore, our management structure reads more like a saga of second chances and recurring themes. Here, team leadership roles are akin to boomerangs, returning to those who’ve tossed them away through micromanagement and a staunch refusal to trust. This skepticism isn’t reserved; it extends from the diligent interns to the backbone of our middle and back office teams, creating a tapestry of oversight so tight it could rival our vintage carpets for complexity.

At the heart of this dynamic is a character whose rise seems fueled not by merit but by a distant camaraderie, rooted in the scenic landscapes of Switzerland. This individual, known for a remarkable Schwabian efficiency, seems to prioritize personal gain over team synergy, notably in the strategic maneuvering of his electric vehicle between meetings to capitalize on the bank’s free charging stations. This daily ritual, performed with the precision of a Swiss watch, stands as a testament not to sustainable practices but to an artful mastery of system navigation for personal benefit.

This scenario underscores a broader challenge within our office ecosystem: the delicate balance between giving second chances and recognizing when new leadership visions are needed. It’s a narrative that adds to our office’s unique character, weaving together tales of perseverance, ambition, and the occasional electric car ballet in the parking lot.

cons: - Any transformation journey such as cloud adoption moves slower than an elephant on an uphill. - Bureaucracy gets in the way of modernization of technology. - In TDI, all tooling support is outsourced to vendors like HCL, DXC who do not take ownership of any service requests assigned to them and there are no SLAs. - On more than one occasion, I was told to interview female candidates only and we ended up compromising on the skill-set of the hired candidate just because management wanted to show gender diversity.

advice: Try to fix the god complex. Local CEO’s and COO’s wield too much power. Matrix system is stupid as some people play with it and others suffer. It’s a significant roadblock for anyone trying to do good work as none of the leaders feel invested and person ends feeling like being on an island alone.
pros: Each team is different so there must be good leaders out there providing excellent work culture to their team mates. Or if one needs to prioritise life over work without long term ambitions.
cons: Poor work culture. Everything seems disconnected and all process improvements are basics mindless data collection exercise without knowing the purpose and strategy. This is across the board. Everyone loves to hide behind “Bank Strategy”, “this is how bank works” and “this is not my job so I don’t want to hear about it”. For senior leaders coming in, it can be frustrating to not have any control over outcome of team’s efforts. There are too many seniors who have learnt the game and have no interest in helping the new joiners as they wait for their retirement with the bank. Despite of multinational claims, the local management acts like they have special rights to get company sponsored benefits. Most will balk at the idea of not getting a hotel / car of their choice eg, will need company resource to fix their network issues while they are on personal travel and would like their teams or relatively junior employees to stand outside their cabin for meetings they organised and seek permission to enter. What they do with their own team is not for me to say but it happens in this day and time itself is worth cringe. Most leaders do a lot of lip service when it comes to leadership while themselves not practising any of that at all IRL. They project themselves as new age leaders but in practice, they have god complex - normally found in leaders of many Indian organisations. Their ideas of how to treat their own team are old generations. While they will also people to take risk and make mistakes and learn from them, in private, they will do exact opposite if someone ends up making a mistake. Their lack of confidence to ask hard questions and demand action from global peers translates into extra pressure on local resources who have been forced to work in a matrix environment where two leaders can’t have an honest conversation with each other.

pros: Deutsche Bank is so large that one can easily know where other open and interesting positions are. From what I have seen, it is not too difficult to move between department, which is a plus. Also there are some nice perks, such as 4 months of maternity leave and unlimited sick days through the year. The bank has a number of DBPerks which gives you discounts from airlines to Apple computers. The fact the Bank is truly global gives your the ability to relocate if you want to. The tuition reimbursement policy is pretty good, and there are also plenty of courses offered by the bank.
cons: There is a lot of bureaucracy and there is not standard of "perks" through the bank. Some departments get certain perks, while others don't. Of course, if you work in the bank offices you don't get as many privileges and it always feels like your job is on the line, or that you are a cost or nuisance. The offices in Midtown are pretty ugly and many people dislike the open architecture. Unfortunately, it seems that's the way many banks are going. Also, the secretarial support is the worst, at least in my department. In general it seems that it is nearly impossible to fire low performing employees, which in my opinion brings down the moral of entire departments. That is truly an unfortunate aspect of the Bank. It may be that this limited to my department, but it should not be the case.

If you can put up with it working here, you'll have a good chance to be poached by a different company.
cons:
The office in Cary is filled with incompetent senior managers.  The least competent is at the top, followed by the management team.  Why?  Because they're cast-offs, or imports from elsewhere.  The ones in banking don't understand software development, and the ones in software are the people fired from middle management of other companies.  

This is honestly a dead-end if you want a career.  They talk about "expert path" for technical people which doesn't exist, at least not in Cary.  You will have no autonomy as all the decisions are made in London and NY.  Your senior manager is put in place by those same teams nervous about hiring outside of the hubs, so his job is just to work you until you quit and not to make any noise such as picking good software or practices.  Your failure provides them cover to not transfer jobs from their location.  They have never promoted anyone in Cary to a senior position- the last three directors weren't even from other Deutsche Bank locations; they went outside the company instead of promote one of the more than 100 existing managers or senior developers.  There is a serious flight of talent- other companies are easily able to poach people who are competent, able to work under pressure, and worth every penny of their salary.  Speaking of which, you used to get a bonus for all the downsides mentioned above.  No more.   It depends on the performance of the company  to get a maximum of 4%.  Take a look at the stock and you'll see how unlikely that is.    Diversity is overdone- protected groups can't be fired, and no one cares to take the time to hire good talent, they just want to have bodies to fill their hiring quotas.  The center head stood up in front of the employees at a town hall and said he's going to hire 50% women. What happened to equal opportunity hiring?   Oh and the fitness center and cafe mentioned as "pro" are just 'meh', but I had to say something nice to fill in that box.  Which is what you'll do for several hours a week- mandatory training classes for financial stuff which you'll never use as a developer but bureaucracy rules.  The HR team is horrible- they live in a little private area, through a card-key door, so you can't interact with them.  If you ask them a question, they'll reply with "call the hotline'.  Everyone desk is a 'trading desk', meaning they've crammed people into huge open areas with the same double-monitor and phone on the side of the desks with employees 5-wide and back to back.  Even call centers have more room.  They've got 800+ people in one building that other residents of the office park have closer to 300 in theirs.  If you need time to concentrate on working out a difficult debugging or clever software solution: give up.  The noise level doesn't allow it (*See working late or weekends comment).  This sardine-like setup also has an unfortunate characteristic of if someone skips a shower, everyone knows it.

advice: Pick a strategy and stick to it. Stop re-orgs at the top for a period and clear out the rot underneath. pros:
If you're on the right team, everything is great. Mobility opportunities, advancement opportunities are plentiful as well - on the right team. Very easy to network with colleagues in other locations to build a personal network that is global. For a strong willed person, it is very easy to flourish.

On the right team, work life balance is perfect. You could not ask for better.

Compensation is great as well for the market, although it will need to be adjusted upwards over the next few years to account for new competitors.

Smart, talented people are the norm.

Very strongly defined set of company values.
cons:
Customer-centricity is the new push as a corporate value, but is little more than lip service on the ground. No KPIs have trickled down from the ExCo as to how this should be measured.

The organization as a whole is too top heavy. Constant emails from different ExCos about people we have no interaction with changing job roles and taking over responsibilities that aren't even obliquely related. This happens almost monthly, to no real benefit.

Constant re-orgs allow incompetent employees to hide and maintain their status. Little to no accountability for teams that manage vendors - the vendors always fail to deliver, and the teams managing them get away with it because of the constant re-orgs.

Tech projects are almost always top heavy. Too many people with no idea about what it takes to build a product involved in the process giving invalid opinions, trying to be the smartest person in the room. Too many meetings, too much design by committee. Projects run over budget and under deliver as a result. Business partners aren't held accountable for the failure and move on to new projects to continue the cycle of ruination.

Obstructionism by teams in other locations doing similar work is common. Land grabs for projects and people occur constantly with the re-orgs, allowing empires to be built. Middle management seems to solely be concerned with owning projects instead of delivering value.

Interaction with the best talent

In the post-pandemic era, Bank can look at a fair distribution of work across the hubs/tech centers instead of investing only in tech centers.
pros:
Great working culture at least among the Banks in Singapore. Work-Life balance is good. Sometimes can get people relaxed and laid back especially in the pandemic era.
Employee Benefits are comprehensive.
Especially for Technology, Engineering Profession is respected. Bank actively promotes Engineering Culture.
cons:
Some divisions, especially in Technology, can be large and distributed. This slows down decision making and getting work done leading to work stress. Although Bank is investing in Modernization, there are far too many legacy systems running on legacy infrastructures.
Singapore, considered a high-cost centre, is not part of the bigger picture in growing technology talent. Hence technology career opportunities in Singapore are limited.

After lehman and ML they are definately going to be one of the top banks on wall street. Senior people can be very demanding, don't do investment banking unless you are ready to give up your life. Overall the pay was amazing, never made so much money in my life, there is alot of favortism towards ivy league graduates. advice: Cut the cord from New York and London. We are perfectly capable of running and developing software well above and beyond the short leash that we've been put on. The politicking needs to end.
