Mgmt is trying to bring more structure and resources
cons:
Pay is good when you first get here, but average to below average
Needs to do a better job of incentivizing employees
Needs more team events
No real sense of culture, siloed work environment
No good sense of what is going on in the business globally...lack of cohesion
Too many internal systems and they are old

summary: Be careful which division and team you choose to apply for.
pros: The bank is decent at recognizing high performers and promoting based on merit.  Depending on the group that you are in, work/life balance is achievable, however, if you are not working overtime you will not be seen as working hard enough.
cons: There is no singular corporate culture.  While this wouldn't necessarily be a bad thing, it results in vast inconsistencies in experience depending on which team, division, or even building you work in.  Unfortunately, if you find that you would like to transfer within the bank, management is able to prevent you from transferring for up to six months.

advice: Show some sponsorship toward the younger people on the desk and maybe they will stop leaving for competitors.
pros: Eat what you kill environment and if you play your cards correctly you can climb the ranks quicker than other sell side shops
cons: Tons of kissing up to the right people despite how good you are...nothing matters unless you cozy up to the right people. Some of the smartest people in the group never get promoted or paid since they can't play politics....

summary: DB Centre on a Death Spiral
advice: Stop hiring from IITs and IIMs. In any case, those grads hardly stay beyond a couple of years.
pros:
- Decent salary, esp for people from Tier 2 colleges
- Good work life balance if aligned to a chill desk 
- Some bright people here and there; but high attrition at junior levels
cons:
- C Grade Middle and Top Management in DBC 
- Extremely top heavy. Old timers are adding zero value and are clinging on for the lack of markatable skills - leading to near-zero attrition at top levels 
- Too much org politics
- Limited mobility within DBC mumbai and to other locations
- Skills you gain are usually not valued outside DBC or are not useful in Indian markets
- Back office culture and mindset
- Bright people have left already. DBC now consists of people who are finding it hard to get out

advice: Plan for long term. Invest in technology. Your shortsightedness to save a few bucks by punishing your employees will cost you more in the long run.
pros: None. This was hell on earth.
cons: There is a distinct lack of responsibility within the company. No one wants to take ownership, and I found that many people were confused about what they should be doing. People join and leave too quickly and no history of why is properly documented and no handoff of who is taking this over is captured (if anyone is even taking over). Additionally, the culture was abysmal. There is very little diversity. Resources are sparse. Better hold on to that pen they gave you the first day, because it's probably the only one you'll get. Hope you have your own hardware that is pared down enough to work with DB's sad tech.

advice: Cultivate a stronger and flatter team culture.
pros: Global firm name and reputation especially given current circumstances.  Foreign-based firms are probably relatively safer and "more stable" than their US counterparts.  This also translated to a greater diversity in the workplace.
cons: Office was very standard and no-frills.  Clear lack of team direction and togetherness with a very tight hierarchy adhered to.  This often translated to lack of motivation and a lot of time being wasted waiting for team members.  Lay-offs were also frequent and a lot of the work experience will revolve around which group you are being placed in, with some groups definitely having a stronger culture than others.

advice: Global HR Head needs to ensure a thorough audit is done on India HR department
pros: Great leaders in Transaction Banking and Retail banking. BKC office premises a treat to work in, houses some of the best restaurants in the suburbs
cons: Hr department hardly works , focuses on politics / good performers have been asked to leave. Poor talent from standard chartered being hired for all VP level and above roles which fall vacant - poor performers / junior external talent being hired at VP plus levels in Hr consistently

summary: Great team, challenging work, company future questionable
pros: The team is built from amazing and smart people, it is a pleasure to work with them. Also the communication with other teams is usually very friendly and cooperative. Salary is very good, work life balance great - the working hours are very flexible.
cons: The company is trying hard for several years to get out of the mistakes of the past, as a result the sentiment towards the company is somewhat negative, year bonus is almost non existent, good people are often leaving for a more perspective job.

summary: Disconnect between upper management and middle managers
advice: Have regular meetings VP level managers and make them part of any significant change to the organizational structure. Reconsider the
pros: There are many opportunities for changing locations and changing your role. The culture is not as cutthroat as some other banks.
cons: There is a disconnect between upper management and middle managers, where upper management is trying to push large initiatives forward just for their own benefit without taking a notice of how this affects managers below them and ultimately the banks performance.

summary: Conservative hierachy but good place to work
advice: The One-Bank culture being pushed seemed superficial, promotion or movement to other areas of the bank was very political. If job opportunities were issued to all staff in an open manner it would improve and motivate more staff.
pros: A fair place to work and management really pushed work life balance for the staff. Financially it was paying at or above market.
cons: Hierachical structure of the bank in the finance department was entrenched. Often had to stay late to finish off reports and systems were not the best.

summary: DB - a solid place to work.
advice: Keep it up.
pros: DB is a seemingly great comany. Senior managment takes its role to develop strategy and communicate to employees very seriously. Generally impressed with the people who I work with or interact with. Compensation is on par or better and the benefits are the best that I have experienced. Lastly, the company takes diversity very seriously.
cons: DB however is a massive firm with over 78k employees. Trying to progress through a firm of this size is difficult without having a great network or through nepotism.

advice: Communicate more.
pros: If your direct manager was great then everything about your job was fantastic.  The benefits were great as was the time off policy.  Managers had a mandatory two weeks off in a row.
cons: The growth potential was horrible.  If you received a promotion in the middle of the year you did not receive any raise until the beginning of the following year.  The communication from top down was very poor as well.  As a manger you sometimes feel like your hands are tied.

summary: Overall Positive but Opportunities of Growth are Limited.
advice: Pay attention to the needs of your people.  Quite a bit of good talent moves on when they see no potential of growth.  The political climate of turning the other cheek needs to change as well.
pros: A global company with an international reach.
cons: Hectic work schedules, to much politics, very few opportunities for growth.  Growth is much easier out of the London or German Offices.  Any other office would be considered a satellite office with very few opportunities to grow.

summary: Great team with strong cross discipline collaboration. But it is, like many others, a broken European bank.
advice: Try your hand at used car sales. Please.
pros: Great team members, good global networking opportunities, and strong franchise in most asset classes.
cons: As it is a broken Euro bank, there is an outsized focus on cost control--every dollar you make for the firm will disappear into a Frankfurt black hole, never to be discussed again. And, as the Japan market is seen internally as a necessary evil, the local managers are the worst sort of shortsighted 'yes men'.

summary: good ficc franchise but not so good pay
pros: great people. still very much has the kind of pre-crisis fratty vibe. one of the top fixed income franchises on the street - ppl take great pride in being part of the franchise
cons: no qualms except comp: pay is roughly around market level (~57k HKD per month) but no housing allowance whereas some other BBs get >65k all-in. Not a huge issue as a junior i suppose but doesnt feel good to know that ur sort of underpaid relative to ur friends at other BBs doing the same job.

advice: Reward support functions well
pros:
Some really great HR policies announced in the last 2 years . People are very nice and helpful and caring. 

The HR department is very good and helpful. They provide good career advice. 

Some of the business managers need to stretch and grow profits
cons:
Compensation levels low especially for support functions and the danger is they might lose good people  in the next couple of years

The company is too hung up on headcount and levels and that is not good for the future of the bank.

summary: Amazing experience and lots of actions.
advice: Recent deskside outsourced management does not not have a clue how to run the business. Please bring back the old management team.
pros: Lots of people to meet with great opportunity to grow. Visited many offices in the US and all the workers are very friendly and helpful.
cons: So many managements and changes that the support team have a hard time following. Recently assigned team leads are a joke. Instead of mentoring and provide supporting for their team member, they are nothing but manager's puppies.

advice: Shareholders have not received profit in over 3 years. Stocks down 30% for this year.. highly recommend removing some of the management team if not most of it and relying on the strong infrastructure of the junior personnel. My team of 12 had 6 managers and that was just the US side.
pros: Good pay and unlimited sick days
cons: Good pay, this is bad as there is NO upward mobility. Thus you are stuck making what you make or take your chances and move to another company. Maybe less pay.

summary: Bad working experience as a minority of a different culture.
advice: Needs to stop the discrimation among minority's within HR.  Too much unfair and bias practices. Change group heads.
pros: Disability benefits are on par. Compensation for the elite is good.
cons: Minorities are not given the opportunity to  excel in the various jobs within HR.  The managers are very good at suppressing progress. Discrimation, Retaliation, suppression, biasnes , unfairness is culture. Managers encourage division and take of "their own".

summary: Incompetent senior management along side staff within their business structure.
advice: Please hire young fresh talent rather some 20 plus years arrogant individual who is only looking towards retirement...at the same time coming from a irrelevant position such as IRS  or other government agency that is oblivious on handling a department etc.
pros: Pay and benefits and work life balance
cons: Very political and socialism hierarchy. A lot of favoritism within one team.  No resources available to learn other than ACAMs which you do on your own. No system in place within their AFC Dept.

advice: Value and invest in the human resources of the company, rather than just looking at the bottom line by cutting cost.
pros: One of the biggest committed market maker - good information from the desks when they are willing to share. Good exposure to institutional investors
cons: VERY inorganized. Penny pinching to the extreme where work process is interrupted. Information sharing seems optional at times, even when it is for the greater good of the company. Short change their employees by hiring them through an outsource consulting firm to maintain a minimum headcount.

summary: Management is way too concerned with job preservation instead of job performance
advice: Get out of your offices and work more with your people instead of staying buried behind computers and spreadsheets then complaining that noboby knows what they're doing
pros:
Lots of employee involvement in community support. 
Flexible working hours.
Casual environment.
Jeans on Fridays.
Time allowed off is decent.
cons:
Management too focused on putting out fires because of outdated technology and procedures.
Local facility has limited autonomy in making any changes to way business is run - most decisions start and end in Europe.

summary: Good brand name, but sometimes a dysfunctional work environment
advice: If you want to play with top tier platforms, focus on rewarding the top performers before they demand the reward...
pros: Broad platform resources and brand name recognition opens doors not otherwise available, better work life balance than most other platforms and some smart colleagues.
cons: Some unhelpful people running around who make it their mission to shoot down any idea. The management's mentality is to pay the minimum to keep people on board, which leaves most people in the mindset that management is constantly trying to take advantage.

advice: Hire managers that can demonstrait they are qualified to manage. Experiance in the field as well as  of the jobs beneath you would be great. Dont nickel and dime every employee when you have no career paths for them to follow. Progress for an employee is only money when there is no path.
pros:
Relaxed managment
Little oversight
Staff is very nice to work with
Paychecks are always paid correctly and on time
cons:
Very little knowledge by those in mgmt
Pay increases are rare
Direction in job function is near non-existant
No training
Corporate atmosphere is very cold

advice: the management did a very good job to run this site under the overall company culture which is very strict. you guys are smart.
pros: it is a very formal, standard bank. It runs by a set of very smart people. Most of the people here are very friendly, not much hassle between employee, and lots of new friends can be made.
cons: Very traditional bank, it has too many rules which make people less productive to a large extends. The technologies used here are not cutting edge at all. The first priority is always safe, secure.

advice:
Don't just say you are open to ideas. Actually listen and implement ideas 
Retain and encourage good ideas by giving less powers to VP and above
pros:
Deutsche bank is actually DBOI in Pune which is technology operations indeed

Some pros:
Great renumeration
Great transport facility
Great infrastructure
Good opportunity to learn about banking
cons:
VP dominance
Lack of strategic direction
Lack of Agile adoption or reluctance to change
Mostly maintenance projects
Expensive canteen
Low salary hikes
No onsite travel opportunity
No 4 wheeler parking for below AVP

advice: Stop going through the motions and commit to the center's started goals. Stop tolerating middle management empire building and infighting. Stop protecting managers who are demonstrably ineffective.
pros:
Smart engineering staff
High salaries
Large bonus pay
cons:
Hours are frankly abusive
Chaotic - frequent total reorgs mean you wrong be working with the team you joined within a year
Most projects are uninteresting and grueling slogs
Politics are by far the rule of the day and hinder nearly all efforts
Local management is fixated on "alpha," a vague term borrowed from banking with little basis in reality for the center

summary: Good experience, grinding work and long hours
advice: Management doesn't evaluate employees on true merit. They back fill evaluations to match the dollars HR tells them then can spend.
pros: It's really good experience with high level clients and lots of responsibility. Good benefits, time off, and lots of extra curricular activities such as sports clubs (they love soccer and golf).
cons: The reason they are in Jacksonville is because they can get quality work at a lower price than in NY and Jersey and it's average financial services pay. It's very much a grind and long hours and can get quite confrontational.

pros: Did well through the crisis, lots of money being poured into tech and electronic trading. Street recognition / reputation way up in last few years because of this effort.
cons: We are taking globalization of support to ridiculous levels. Outsourcing critical tech jobs is materially hurting us. Seems to come and go as senior mgt changes. Current mgt outsources as an easy way to save money. Next mgt will see that it doesn't work and localized key teams. And the vicious cycle continues.

summary: Back office, good pay, limited exit oppos
advice: Take an active interest in the human capital invested here. That would go a long way forward in ensuring that people are equipped to handle responsibilities and assume leadership roles.
pros:
Compensation, work-life balance

Compensation by general standards is really high. The sad bit is that it doesn't compare much to the front office. Being a back office, the office is slightly shielded from cycles in the economy.
cons: Exit opportunities are limited. Attrition rate is really high. Little scope of movement to front office jobs within DB. Management does not seem very investment in their juniors.

summary: Nice, smart colleagues. Demanding tasks and international climate.
advice: Focus on top tier universities.
pros: Reputation in the field of investment banking. Deutsche Bank is a large corporation with presences in many countries and conseuquently great opportunities for international assignments. Due to being an universal bank, there are multiple business areas.Smooth day, multi task keeps the day flowing and you have the chance to learn something new every day. Senior management is great to work with; also willing to teach you new things, at least once. Communication is great.
cons: HR seems to be unorganized.

summary: operations: 1st job out of college, good experience, poor management
advice: reconsider the business model; think strategically as the people make the company and bring the bank's success;
None to my direct management as they are doing well. Continue to streamline processes and operations. New CEO now will be interesting to see what he does.
pros: Smart, friendly and collaborative colleagues in my area, Fantastic manager that really looks out for his employees while providing solid direction and guidance. Good work/life balance. Many active employee network groups that hold fun events.
cons: Very large and inefficient in general. It Takes too many different groups and way too much time to get things done. Very open seating arrangement.

advice: Continue to work with employees and teams to build on what systems you have, to better stream line processes around trading, back office, risk and compliance
pros: Great people, surrounded by very smart people, deep culture, client focus, strong compliance, strong support system, environment build for people to achieve as much as they feel they can.
cons: sometimes, since some of the systems are patched together from a host of several firms that DB has acquired over the years, technology can be a bit finicky.

pros:
- Brand
- Y/E appraisals
- fun and sports events
- open door policy: AVP's/VP's listen what you say. No matter how it goes, maybe in your favour or against.
cons:
- alot of management changes and policies change has lead to a different direction
-  if location is Jaipur, dont expect a good experience in terms of location, infrastructure and food. Pathertic food conditions
- cost reductions and emplyees layoffs has led chaos
- bonus is as per management and if you are their fav, no matter how you are rated you will get good bonuses. else chillarrrr

advice: While merit based reviews are a good start, don't adjust the bar when it is convenient.  Management should value their infrastructure support and development group as much as they do their investment group.  Arbitrary forced ranking of performance should never occur, though it is a common occurrence.
pros:
Lots of mobility opportunities
Hi intellect for most employees
Good compensation
cons:
Lots of talk about change, but nothing really changes
Ask for your lifetime salary requirements upfront since your base is not likely to go up EVER
Internal processes can be maddening

summary: Great work life balance, little rewards
advice: There needs to be a clearer way to evaluate and reward staff running projects under Vice President level. If this cannot change, there should provisions to allow for Vice Presidents to be placed in countries like Tokyo without having to be a manager.
pros: Great work life balance that allows for shifted work hours (within core hours) and working from home when needed. This caters for families with small children.
cons: No individual performance evaluation for staff below Vice President. This means that no matter how many projects we complete, we are not rewarded for our work.

summary: Not a good time to join
advice: Hurry up with infrastructure overhaul and stop dithering on required cost cutting.
pros: Great people, plenty of project opportunities. Business is very innovative. New Ceo is promising but challenge to overhaul may be too great.
cons: Very fragmented infrastructure. Company grew too quickly. Poor data quality. Overly bureaucratic + slow decision making, so much needed change is very slow and demoralising. Needs to cut costs but does not know how / unable to execute. Overhang of litigation and decision to reduce pay to compensate for this is highly demoralising.

summary: Don't waste your career in this place
advice:
First change the dinosaurs that have been in the management role for such a long time. They are not bringing any value besides moving people from role to role. 
The same Managers don't want to deal with internal platforms built in Europe which are already efficient. They would rather spend more money building something for the US because they don't want to deal with Developers overseas.
Those systems have been launched into production when they FAILED a testing process.
Bring the process where Analyst, Associates, AVPs, provide feedback about their managers. Make it both ways. 
I had a manager that treated their employees wrong (raised to HR) and still got promotes to a higher role! Why, how?
Add competent people to run the operations in Jax. How come they wanted to bring employees to the office in the middle of a pandemic?

The Company have had a cutting cost approach for a few years. Why no raise when the CEO gets a 40%+ increase on his salary?
pros:
Good office environment
Free coffee and tea
cons:
Bureaucracy
No RAISE in 3 years! Keep trending in this company. They don't want to keep up with inflation. People are loosing money every year while working here
A lot of turnaround - good talents are leaving every time
Top management only want to implement systems that are on top of other systems to justify their high paycheck
For promotions they have a mystery Panel (nobody knows who they are and/or which departments they work for).
For promotions the best way is to leave and come back in a few months applying for a higher role, otherwise it takes a few years.
Terrible bonus ! its always a percentage of the percentage.... Let's say the bonus is 4% of your salary, at the end of the year the higher I've seen is the 50% of the 4%. Literally a 2% bonus.
During the pandemic the company provided zero support for their employees. They saved money by not having anyone going into the office and they could no provide help to set up their workers at home.
On month three or four after the pandemic started they wanted people to come to the office. The operations manger is clueless of what a pandemic is.
Fixing issues depends on a lot of people where 50% of them will care, the other 50% will ignore all your requests bc its not part of their role.

advice: - Take action on restructuring rapidly and move back to focus on growth
pros:
- Diverse range of roles, and hence opportunities. Onus on the employee to make use of this
- Bright people
- Good compensation, though becoming less so relative to peers as time passes
- Good benefits (additional leave; parental leave)
cons:
- Undergoing a period of transition and restructuring. Currently painful for employees
- Years of negative press and reduced compensation (relative to peers) have impacted staff morale
- High expectations for staff, in particular to work outside normal business hours. Impacts work-life balance

advice: I am a dedicated hardworking youngest corporate banking manager working with Deutsche bank India since 4 years. Would love to join Deutsche bank Canada in order to enhance my skills and set and take few new challenges.
pros: One of the leading bank across the globe, performing required corporate social responsibilites in order to keep internal external clients happy along with it's stake holders
cons: Deustche has limited branches they should look for some expansion. Human resources manager should be more helpful in putting suitable candidate to overseas requirements.

advice: Weed out the old school people who do things as 'that's the way it's always been done'. Whom also subscribe to old school banking culture rather than the digital mindset.
pros: I have been very well cared for by Deutsche Bank post a serious issue requiring multiple surgeries. My manager and HR take looking after people very seriously and I commend them for that.
cons: Outdated systems/ processes that are slow and incredibly bureaucratic making being innovative hard. However, this is in response to all the fines and it is hard to see how this will change (although they are trying).

summary: Bank culture is good but too much power to managers which demotivates real talented team members
advice: Be more vigilant and involved with to the last one in the queue as they are the real ones who make the work done. Don't blindly believe corrupt middle level manager who are corrupt to the core and even involve in money transactions for promotion and staying long with Bank
pros:
Good benefits
Work life balance
Good renumeration
cons:
No proper management
Too much power given to managers and higher management don't bother about lower level employees

summary: Decent place to work but beware of offshoring...
advice: I would say they are doing a great job, at least better than US peers.  My advice to them is continue to marketing campaign which is resonating quite well with new grads.
pros: DB is a great name, particularly outside the US.  I joined the GTO graduate training class and we had 6 weeks of training on London which was sweet.  Training and work is obviously different...
cons: Offshoring was happening before the crisis and i imagined that just got worst...  I heard controlling jobs are going as well

advice: This place is so poorly managed I am surprised it hasn't cost the bank millions of dollars. Oh wait it has.
pros: Good benefits and lots of PTO
cons: Terrible pay and you will be treated as if you are incompetent or lazy. You will be working in a production environment which means the numbers are the only thing that matter. If you 3 or less days of PTO your numbers will not be adjusted and you will have to make up the time when you get back. If you take a sick day your numbers will not be adjusted. If you spend the day in training or mandatory meetings your numbers will not be adjusted. Plan on working every weekend.

summary: Highly Professional and Great Place to work with
advice: Please keep a check in certain areas of work, especially with some specific senior managers and practices being carried out, to build a healthier environment and safe place to work for the employees.
pros: Professionalism, with good knowledge sharing sessions, team dynamics, new things to learn, in all good place to work at.
cons: Some better approach / policies required to deal in certain cases with the higher management, and some wrong practices being conducted needs to be taken care of promptly and properly, to avoid any further harm to the organization.

summary: Great place to start your career as an engineer.
pros: Very smart people to work with, interesting projects (at least if you're an engineer) and a nice office space. It's a great place if you're a junior engineer and want to start you career. You'll learn all the essentials that help you to deliver large-scale and complex IT solutions. Very cool (local) senior management.
cons: No career opportunities for senior engineers. You either become a manager or have look for opportunities outside of the company. Definitely too much bureaucracy and a lot of cost-cutting and travel freezes over the last years.

advice: Need to start listening to ground realities in terms of compensation. Also need to act more professional.
pros: Work freedom. Great place for employees in senior positions and the ones with family. Good work life balance. Low cost of living.
cons: Compensation way below industry average. HR and management in jacksonville not professional. Treat employees as expendable, specially the ones from overseas. Platform way too top heavy so very low bonus compensation for new comers. At best good for a year or so.

advice: Continue to invest in operational improvements to maximize employee productivity and improve client experience. Invest in top young talent by offering better performance based compensation structures.
pros: Great company with many development opportunities for individuals that work hard and take initiative. Despite the large company size, change is very much supported at DB. The benefit offering is good.
cons: Experience is sometimes overvalued by upper management above performance. Compensation for entry-level analysts is on the lower end of the scale, which makes it difficult for the company to recruit and keep top-talent.

advice: What goes around comes around.
pros: Good playground for politics. Best place to work if you have network. Interns paradise. Tricks of trades are best learned here. Best place to work to get career lessons. People who are good at psychophant stays here long.
cons: High tech innovative ideas/ambitions but low on output , Save ur neck attitude of management. Fruits(bonus) is shared at top at expense of engineers. Every team has at-least two scapegoats to hack at performance reviews. No work life balance.

summary: Director Private Wealth Management Mortgage Operations
advice: Recognize that line level employees do not have skills necessary to  cover for unfilled higher positions.. When meeting one-on-one with a highly skilled, productive member of the Reg Support staff, CH, find something positive to say , NOT "you talk too much during conference calls". And then wonder why she resigned to accept another position
pros: Benefits, Generous annual leave. Jacksonville has a low cost of living
cons: COO Management is removed from the day-to-day  operation. Reg Support is an obstacle, rather than offering support. Operations is chronically under-staffed.

advice: Continue to invest in people and weed out negative poor performers
pros:
Refreshing to work with the new avatar of the HR team

They are making a big difference with the positive attitude without the baggage of the past

Focused in solutions and working in a collaborative manner to make it an even more engaged workplace

Earlier HR team was lazy, short sighted lacking vision.

Great place to learn
cons:
Compensation needs catching up
Leverage technology more
Respond to changes in the external market quicker
Need to build processes with end user in mind

advice: Clean house in the middle manager ranks. If someone cannot reduce their inflated cost to meet the objectives then remove them.
pros:
Great people and a compelling vision for transforming the bank.
Great pay, but there is a reason for that.
cons:
Leadership is rewarded for the wrong criteria, size of teams, budget, not value they generate.
Highly political organization, Who you know is the most important factor for promotions and opportunities.
Location strategy is badly broken. After years of trying we still hire developers in the most expensive cities in the world.

summary: Good first job if you’re not looking for many exit opps
advice: Be honest about what the job is, don’t seek out ambitious, innovative thinking people and try to put them in a box
pros:
Training in London 
Good financial training overall
Salary/ benefits employer math 
Good people (not mgmt)
cons:
Massive, old dinosaur of Wall Street I don’t see it being around in 5-10 years 
still lots of clean up from 2008, horrible clients mgmt, unfettered capitalistic greed 
Little mobility for younger people because people stay so long, senior positions beneath basically exec board level roles are only marginally different than middle tier

advice: Stay the course for at least 18 months with a given technology program and management team so that something tangible can be delivered
pros: Diversity of work force; stimulating to work in such a complex matrix of multiple cultures.  People in the trenches are very down to earth and try to deliver value despite the convoluted processes needed to get things done in IT
cons: Constant re-orgs means re-branded objectives.  You end up wasting energy every time you have to start over under a new manager.  Now all jobs moving to NC and FL

advice: Learn to build on what has already been done and use that to your advantage not reinvent the wheel every time.
pros: Good ideas and a vision of where they want to go and where they want to be in the investment banking community.
cons: Poor implementation as everyone in management seems to want to start from the beginning.  I worked for a few different managers, each who wanted to throw out everything that had been accomplished preciously and start brand new.  Are you kidding?  How many times are we "analyzing" the same thing?

advice: Don't give up on fighting to be productive.  Try to keep employees motivated.
pros: Deutsche Bank treats it's employees well.  Most who work here have a good work/life balance, but really it depends on your team and management.  Pay and benefits are competitive.  My current manager is wonderful, and cares about me and my career.  I generally feel like I'm contributing to the company.  Nice building and desk layout.  Mostly interesting people.  Good communities.
cons: We are slowed by regulations and compliance.  Some things that should be easy are hard to do at the bank, like installing free software.

summary: Job at Deutsche Bank Centre Mumbai
advice: Senior management off late is not as visionary and energetic as used to be a few years ago.
pros: Gives you opportunity to engage with global trading and ibanking staff and add direct value to global business. Excellent IIT, IIM background of all peers. Politics is minimum and as long as you keep delivering, you get a very good growth. I worked there for 9 years.
cons: DB Centre in Mumbai doesn't have all roles very exciting so be careful what you are offered. And one does reach a ceiling after a few years because one can't do all functions sitting in this offshore entity.

advice:
Networking is key and expose yourself to as much fixed income knowledge to sell yourself
Make your voice known so you don't get taken advantage of.
pros:
Good balance of work and personal life
Very Hands-on (job allows opportunities learn and expand your knowledge of the different products)
Very structured yet laid back environment
cons:
Difficult to get promotions and very competitive for managemnt roles.

I feel that employee morale at Deutsche Bank has gotten to be pretty low. The perception, even among employees has been that Deutsche Bank has not performed as badly as its competitors throughout the credit crisis. This view was badly shaken with the mass lay-offs that have been occurring in recent months. Some of the blame lies with senior management who have not been forthcoming about communicating the extent of the problems within investment banking and about addressing the layoffs. In my group for example, when people were laid off, it almost seemed as if nothing happened. People even within the group refused to talk about what was going on and this just contributed towards the lack of communication that already existed. 

The hours in investment banking were also a killer. 100+ hour weeks were not uncommon. Furthermore, my group was plagued with the problem of "face-timing". Even if you had no work, you had to show that you were working at least until 11pm each night just to avoid getting ridiculous staffings for projects that some MD cooked up. 

The learning experience was not as great as I hoped it would be. People simply working on endless pitches with really interesting deals few and far between.

Great benefits. Health, dental, and vision plans are excellent. For a company in the US, there are lots of vacation days (over 4 weeks).

cons:
Frustrating experience dealing with work computers and tech programs/tools. The computers are really locked down and it's often difficult to find the right tools for the job that aren't years out of date (I've seen this process improving, but slowly). There is little flexibility in choosing your tools for any particular technical task (it's not an option to install what you like). GitHub is blocked for most people.

Abundance of middle management. I've been on a team consisting of half managers and half workers. Certainly not every team is like this, and it's probably a result of being a large place.

There is a severe lack of technical knowledge among large amounts of employees (working in a software development environment). Many people aren't skilled enough to do their jobs well. One example: a manager on my team doesn't trust automated regression testing (they are not technically knowledgable about the development process) so even though we have a fully automated regression testing suite, people are required to *manually* test everything in releases before managers will approve the release, soaking up large amounts of time and resources. Knowledge of the basics should be expected, as it's a software development center. As a developer, is can be extremely frustrating to deal with so many people who don't know a thing about coding or development or computers at all, but are still supposed to work in a technical job.

Recognition and compensation is often largely tied to who you know, and less about how much of a difference you make. Of course, many people received what they deserved or even more, but for every person I know has been compensated/promoted fairly, I know another who was not at all compensated what they should have been. Which position you find yourself in isn't predictable.

pros: Working in Operations at Deutsche Bank for over 20 years has been an experience.  Operations teams always completed the work with pride and integrity, be it in Trade Finance, Global Markets or Transaction Banking and through the years I worked with many great people and had several good managers.
cons:
Over the years there were many senior executives that led Deutsche Bank, providing a strategic direction which never seemed to change - reduce expenses again and again.  Getting raises, bonuses and promotions was always difficult.  This direction led to moving U.S. dollar processing and account balances to servers in Germany, outsourcing work to vendors and lower cost areas in India, accompanied by a loss of qualified experienced staff in the U.S.  The results - complaints by clients, increased risks and scrutiny by regulators.  Eventually, clients left and regulators questioned the lapses in controls, which lead numerous fines including $630 million for Laundering Russian Money, $2.5 billion for the U.S. and U.K. plus €725 million for Libor Interest Rate Scam, $258 million for Violation of US Economic Sanctions, $7.2 billion for the Sale of Toxic Securities Leading up to the Financial Crisis and $205 million for Violations of New York Banking Laws stemming from Foreign Exchange Trading Business.  The value of the stock declined from $150 in 2007 to the $8.00 neighborhood today.

When people ask me about The Big Short (2015) in reference to Deutsche Bank, I reply Independence Day (1996) is a more appropriate representation, where aliens came to take all available resources and wreak havoc before they move on to the next target.

advice:
A global strategy and 'one-bank' approach is a good idea on paper, but in reality Deutsche Bank might operate more effectively if there was more internal competition. In particular DB-SOA approved applications and departments are stifling creativity and often creating artificial barriers to innovation.

Additionally, there should be reward for loyalty, particularly amongst the high performers and key personell. We're losing too many good people, and whether it's opportunities, the working culture or simply dollars and cents enticing them away, mor needs to be done to keep these people onboard. Whilst India might have a great future, the vast amount talent and business remains in the established offices, and they should not be neglected.
pros:
Deutsche Bank is a truly global player, with a hugely diverse workfoce, financial products and opportunities. Exposure to numerous cultures, backgrounds and working methodologies means that any time here can contribute greatly to personal growth, your CV/Resume and career path. The working conditions are generally good, most people work reasonable hours and work/life balance is taken seriously by most managers. 

I think the benefits are competetive, internal training and learning is abundant and encouraged, and support for external education is good, as long as it is seen to benefit your current role. There is a process for internal movement, which works fairly well, especially when the market conditions are favourable.

Many of the more senior managers within the organisation are very talented and decisive. Once an initiative is kicked off, it's rarely done half heartedly. Strategic vision is well communicated and often executed regardless of resistance or pain.
cons:
Such a huge organisation is often riddled with confusing and sometimes unecessary beaurocracy - it's a truly 'German' bank in that sense. A one size fits all approach to process and strategy is sometimes unhelpful when trying to push through critical changes rapidly. 

There are also still too many middle-aged, unskilled employees, particularly in the US and Continental Europe (this is not the case in London or Asia-Pacific) who tend to be obstructive and miserable. Many of these have been pushed out via outsourcing, but too many remain in lower/middle management roles.

Compensation can range from being market-leading to insulting. If you stay much beyond 5 years, you're likely to fall very far behind the market and although this is probably true of many companies, at DB there is an almost complacent attitude towards this issue. It results in a brain-drain amongst the most dynamic middle-managers (VP/Director) especially if they have come up from Associate or AVP level at the bank. It also means the dead-wood I mentioned earlier are even less likely to be pushed out.

Finally the outsourcing of many roles lead to a collapse of moral in many parts of operations, especially in NY and London. Although much of the basic work is done outside of the high-cost locations, such as Bangalor and Mumbai in India, Birmingham in the UK and soon Jacksonville, FL, the real glue behind the work remains in the hands of a few over-worked and under-valued people who have stayed behind to pick up the peices.

summary: There's a reason (or fifty) why it's the laughingstock of the banking industry

pros: They lure candidates in with good pay and benefits
cons: Where to begin, you could quite seriously write a dissertation on the poor career quality at this place. I have been in the Jacksonville office for 4 years and have seen countless scenarios of amazing performers being turned down for the ONCE A YEAR promotion process (no you cannot be promoted outside of this annual process) to Associate/AVP etc due to politics and department caps, yet absolute garbage employees being hired for Associate/AVP externally. Your entire job here is soul sucking because you spend all day every day fixing "breaks" between systems that the company is too cheap to properly implement. There is no IT here, only clerks in India with a poorly written manual and a manager demanding they close out the work ticket. Constant reorgs trying to figure out how to fix the myriad of issues yet they only serve to give certain people promotions while the others suffer and are left confused as to who they report to. At the end of the day you just have MORE bosses. Toxic work environment where the managers won't even talk to you or acknowledge your existence unless you quit, then they get upset because once again they have to go through the painful round of hiring a candidate which due to company bureaucracy takes between 3-4 months. If you are applying here don't give notice until just before your start date or you could go without a paycheck for months. A lot of people just quit the department to go to a competitor in town BEFORE bonuses were even paid out, that speaks for the desperation to leave and the sub par quality of bonuses. There is zero recognition for hard/above and beyond work because either your manager will take credit or simply no one cares. Once again only those favorites will get a promotion. Complete mismatch between companies stated values and actual quality of work. The department also makes the foolish mistake of only having one person trained on a unique role so that if you decide to move internally you will be stuck training your replacement for months on end, or if you quit they beg you to train your external replacement, who won't start for months.....Maybe other departments are okay to work for but certainly not product control or whatever they decided to name themselves today. If you are a manager elsewhere looking to hire a DB employee don't look down on the fact that someone here hasn't been promoted, chances are they deserved to be many times over, DB just doesn't promote promotions.... You can't even begin to explain how poor the work environment is here, you just have to witness it. Or maybe ask around.....

advice: Understand technologists
pros:
A few intelligent people
high comparable salaries

The center is in a constant state of flux of hire and mostly fire.  In the past year almost the entire leadership team has either been fired or departed and what is left is almost constant haggling amongst middle management to own teams and step into dead mens shoes, regardless of being qualified.

The bank has chosen a SAS import who is completely uninterested in what we are doing and creates authority through fear leaving most quaking and the rest kissing it.  Most of us are unclear how this guy does as we take all of our direction from the London domain leads.  I'm sure he is as nervous about his own position as we are so he is kissing his respected asses and not delivering utility down to us.  Then we have a hired a Chief Development Officer - what Development is this role responsible for and where is the proven calibre?

Our recent town hall said it all: we want to "reverse the pyramid" which means our management are fixated in adhering to organizational shape over finding the right people then incentivizing the good people to stay.  

This week a further 15 heads were culled, which followed similar exercises over the past 5 months leaving many scared about their future.  Why not take a look at why these people didn't achieve success and question whether the organization provides an environment where success is achievable without politics and back-stabbing??

I do not believe Deutsche Bank understands the locality or the technology profession.  Let's say it possibly did at one time, now this is in full reverse.  We started with a message of work/life balance, a table tennis table and a relaxed dress code and now the latter being recently stripped so we look nice for our new New York matrix managers who have no clue about what makes technology people tick.  North Carolina is not about double-breasted suits, politics and "greed is good" - if we wanted this we would get paid a lot more to live in New York.  

There are so many other technology companies to work for in Raleigh.  My entire team is talking aloud about interviewing elsewhere which means this place is heading south.

summary: Don’t come here if you’re a woman
advice:

But don’t think that women are quitting to “spend time with their kids”. They are quitting because they aren’t getting paid, promoted or recognized for the hard work their doing and are treated like second-class citizens in the office. Out of the 10 women in my group (out of 100 people), 3 have quit and 3 more are almost out the door. Not a coincidence...
pros: Can’t think of anything to say

If you’re a woman, you will be underpaid for the same job done as a man, but they will always find an excuse as to why you’re not doing the same job.
You will be cut off in the middle of speaking up at a meeting
Men will disagree with every decision you’ve made, even though they have made the same decision in the past and they will fight you on it
Let’s not even talk about getting promoted
Group heads don’t care about their teams - except for the ones that are constantly in their offices or their buddies
Don’t keep open bottles of water on your desk because the ball being tossed around the trading floor will knock it over and everyone will laugh at you when you get angry. And do they realize that they’re yelling to each other when the ball is being thrown around? Is this a locker room or a place of business?
You will also be told that you’re difficult b/c you try to fight for your position, or not hungry to fight for new business b/c you’re not aggressive enough. So what am I? Difficult or passive?
As a woman, you do all the work to put docs and presentations together, schedule the meetings, etc, but it’s the man who gets to present everything...in other words, you do all the work but get none of the credit; or sometimes you get called out for the one thing that you didn’t do rather than the 99 things that you did do - all by yourself 
As a woman, it’s impossible to get junior men to do work for you
And it’s impossible to bring up any of these issues with senior mgmt for fear of retaliation

This year again the CEO is the second best paid banking CEO and employees continue to suffer. Minimalistic hikes for people. There is a 4 % group variable that too is never paid in full. Seniors have some variable component.
2. Your onshore boss is too worried about his job. He'll do whatever he's asked to do. The focus is only on cost cutting. Nothing else. There is no strategy. They did this last year now their revenues are shaky. Most of the lunch conversation is around who left or has been asked to leave. India is possibly better off though but there have been cuts which are all hush hush. Some percentage of the population is asked to look for a new role or leave without any good reason.
3. There are no backfills. They say they've improved processes and the IT looks better now so there is no need to hire. The truth of the matter is they never did a lot of investment on IT or process improvement, they don't have the money. The result is teams as big as a couple of dozens reduced to a half a dozen people. Your boss tells you that " you should be happy you have a job". Poor chap also clocked in the same time as me. No one is safe. 
4. The HR is useless. I just see them in the canteen. They should speak to the employees more often. Especially in a situation like this when they are withdrawing cab facilities and LnD budgets. I don't remember if I know who my HRBP was. This was specially required to alleviate fears when the Deutsche commerzbank merger news started coming out. With Deutsche bank you should always believe in rumors. Don't believe any of their official communication. Employees value stability, atleast HR can attempt to comfort them in this regard.
5. The overall atmosphere is very depressing. Career development is the last thing anyone wants. They sell all problems as opportunities which is a good way too stretch your people. But there is no growth in any form.. Monetary or hierarchical. People were promoted this year, but it was a retention policy for older poorly paid employees as they'd announced no bonuses again. A lot of good employees lost in the bargain. These people are on the look out now, something DB should curb.
6. India barring Mumbai CIB centre is a  back/middle office for DB. Their IT ops are also based out of these places. The works not that great and most good work happens out of their business hubs across the globe. Mumbai is primarily trading assistant / outsourced front office work.

summary: No Leadership, No Training, No Help
pros: Job is obtainable at a decent salary even if you aren't qualified.
cons:
Many of us were lied to about what the job was when we were hired. The original job posting was for an Automation Engineer. They put us in IT Support. This caused so many people to quit that all the teams are short staffed and overworked. Now that the old site manager is gone and a new one is hiring with honest postings, no one actually wants the job. Probably why they lied in the first place.
Management is a joke, there's no plan, no training, no one helps each other, especially between regions. It's basically the uppers complaining about things until someone hopefully fixes it. They roll over when other teams push back, which means there's no consistency in how to operate, and no documentation to refer to how it's actually supposed to run.
Everyone is so swamped with work that there's no time to do the 'Automation' job that we were supposedly being hired to do. It's just user support issues. They took away the level 1 support so now both jobs fall on the production teams. Tasks that should be handled by the devs are also on the production team, again because the leadership just rolls over and doesn't stand up for their team.
On the occasion someone manages to get on a call with the uppers to raise concerns. Their solution is to stop having those calls with the teams. Mention this to the site managers and they laugh and do nothing about it. And they wonder out loud (again complaining instead of planning) why everyone is quitting.
No one is willing to help each other. There's no training. There's nothing to learn. The things you waste your afternoon talking about that's supposed to be 'training' never get used.
There's no documentation, not even for the users, who come to you constantly for advice on how to use a program you didn't make. You get yelled at for not resolving issues that you can't fix. You get yelled at for doing something that you thought was policy because someone complained so that's not policy anymore. You're constantly on the hook for another teams work that you're waiting on, and there's no accountability if they don't fix the issue because again, leadership just rolls over.
The people you work with a nice enough, because we're all in it together, but I don't know a single person there that's happy to work at Deutsche Bank.

summary: Depressing !! Needs serious and urgent revamp.
advice: If there are any actions taken from your level to fix the system, then nothing has changed at the ground level. Remote control model never works especially where there is conflict of interests. Better initiatives need to be taken to empower local management at every location. There is abundance of good talent in the bank which is currently frustrated and wasted due to politics. Appropriate platform should be provided to help talented employees reach beyond the hurdles created by their respective group management and prove themselves at the larger level. The current Internal mobility process is highly ineffective and mostly ends up with the employee vindictively paying a very high price just for choosing to move to a different project. In the current scenario, ideal talented employees who would act in accordance with our values, would find themselves at the bottom of the performance chart.
pros: Competitive compensation, Brand name, Global presence
cons:
Depressing is the only word that comes to mind while sharing my more than 6 years of experience with this company. Despite being a high performer, there is no scope for growth. DB (especially Cary location) is a big NO NO for people with talent. In fact, they are the most unsuited species for its culture. Most of the power controls are in London and NY and they have vested interests in not letting Cary grow. Someone with good potential is targeted, mistreated, given worthless work and eventually forced to quit by exercising their political might. Most of the management (Directors & VPs) are undeserving loyalist who are only rubber stamps, taking orders from their bosses in NY or London and in return they survive the job (and even get promoted). This is helped by the HB2 hiring freeze and the bank's cost cutting measures which limited the growth in Cary. The technical architects (most of them controlling from London & NY) are highly incapable to even designing basic systems but are given a free hand because of their proximity to those who matter at the cost of quality. You can even find vendors architects & managers dominating and mistreating FTEs only because of support they hold from the powerful. Most of the applications in the bank are outdated and badly designed to handle today's needs. The HR and the senior management is well aware of this but has done nothing except for mentioning it in a couple of town halls & interact sessions. On the contrary, starting last year, even the authority of deciding the recognition award & promotion candidates in Cary was given to London & NY panels. This was a final nail in the coffin for Cary's sovereignty to retain good talent and do what is good for them.
To conclude, the overall atmosphere in the bank is highly political and counterproductive where talented new joiners will only add to a mass of frustrated zombies found everywhere throughout the centre now-a-days.

The on boarding process is nonexistent here so you have to struggle mightily when you first start.
